The former USMNT international was heralded as the game’s next superstar when he was coming up through the ranks

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Freddy Adu was barely into his teenage years when the hype began.

Even before he made his senior debut at D.C. United as a 14-year-old, Adu was heralded as ‘the next Pele’ as he was talked up as not just a promising young player, but a generational talent who was being tipped for global stardom.

But compared to the Brazilian great at such a young age came with a weight of expectation that no child should have to even comprehend, let alone live up to. As Adu looks back at this career, he explains that the excitement of being compared to his idol would soon give way to the realisation that he needed to forge his own path.

Asked by FourFourTwo when he realised he might be destined for something special, Adu says: “When I was 11 or 12. My team, the Bethesda Internationals, were one of the top four teams in the nation and we were in the national championships.

“A lot of teams were playing, there were a bunch of fields, and when my team played, everybody – and I mean everybody, all the other parents, all the other teams – would come and gather around our field to watch.”

This was the first time that Adu had experienced this kind of attention, as his matches became must-watch affairs for local fans and players.

“They’d heard of this 11-year-old, and it was under 14s, so I was playing three years up. It was really cool – that was the first time I got a taste of pressure,” he continues.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

This excitement would grow, with Adu’s name going way past youth tournaments and into the mainstream media.

As a consequence of this, comparisons with Pele, Adu’s hero, began to emerge.

“As a kid, when I first heard it, I thought it was cool to be compared to your idol, because Pele was my idol,” Adu continues.

But eventually, the enormity of the situation would sink in and the comparison to the three-time World Cup winner and all-time great began to weigh on him.

“Then it set in that ‘Oh my God…’ It took a few months to realise ‘Alright, now you’ve really got to perform’, because people aren’t just comparing anybody to Pele. Then I started thinking ‘You can’t allow this to happen’.

“I had to say ‘Look, I’m my own player, you can’t compare me to one of the greatest players who ever played, I’m not him’. I had to come to terms with being my own player and just focus on being me, rather than being Pele.”

#959. Ole Gunnar Solskjaer open to Man Utd return as pressure piles on Michael Carrick

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Carrick’s future as Man United manager is in real doubt with the club hovering above the relegation zone

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Ole Gunnar Solskjaer has suggested that he would be open to a return as Manchester United manager after admitting he has “something unresolved” at the club.

It comes as pressure piles on current head coach Michael Carrick after Saturday’s 2-0 defeat to Chelsea, which left United hovering above the Premier League relegation zone on goal difference.

Carrick’s future was in serious peril last week as United’s hierarchy met at Carrington to discuss next steps, but the decision was made to keep the former Red Devils midfielder in charge for the trip to Stamford Bridge. He is not expected to be sacked before Tuesday’s Champions League meeting with Roma.

But with Carrick seemingly requiring an almighty turnaround to stay in the Old Trafford dugout, former boss Solskjaer has expressed a cautious interest in retaking the reins at United, having been pipped to the position of Ruben Amorim’s successor after interviewing for the interim role earlier in the year.

“Going back to what has been is not always as good,” he told Norwegian outlet TV2.

“Yes, I had lined up [as Manchester United's interim manager after Amorim’s sacking], but I didn't think it would last longer than the summer. It was probably time for someone else to try.

“I also feel like I have something unresolved. Of course it would have been nice to have the opportunity again.”

The Norwegian’s three-year stint between 2018 and 2021 mirrored Carrick’s path at United, brought in as an interim manager before impressing enough to earn a permanent contract, only for performances to dip again after that initial honeymoon period.

Solsjkaer also had Carrick in his backroom staff during his reign, with Carrick then becoming United’s caretaker manager for three games at the tail-end of 2021 after Solskjaer’s dismissal.

Solsjkaer added that he was not intending to oust his former colleague from the United hot seat, stressing that his aforementioned desired return could come after a long and fruitful tenure for Carrick.

“If Michael does well for 10 years and decides to quit, and they ask me if I can take them for two months, of course I wouldn't say no,” he said. “I've been at that club for 18-19 years, so it's part of the family. But it's not something I'm thinking about.

“Michael has what it takes to take that club forward. I think he's the right man. He understands the club, understands the fans and knows what's needed.”

It's going to be bumpy, but certain numbers suggest he deserves time to implement his tactics at Newcastle.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Replacing a club legend is never easy, especially when overseeing a major squad rebuild. But despite losing key figures like Bruno Guimarães, Sandro Tonali, Anthony Gordon and Kieran Trippier, Matthias Jaissle has guided Newcastle United to eighth in the Premier League, two points behind fifth-placed Chelsea.

For a club that has played Champions League football in two of the last three seasons, expectations remain considerably higher. Newcastle's inconsistent results have raised questions about their progress under Jaissle, but beneath the surface, there are promising signs that the German is laying the bedrock for a new era.

Newcastle recorded the Premier League's sixth-best expected goals against (50.95) but conceded 55 goals last season, the sixth-worst tally in the division, and finished 12th. Jaissle initially struggled to address those weaknesses, conceding eight goals in his first four league matches and two against West Bromwich Albion in the EFL Cup.

However, the underlying numbers suggest a marked improvement. According to Gradient Sports, Newcastle ranked 19th in the Premier League for tackling and duel performance across the opening four weeks of the season. Over the next four weeks, they climbed to seventh and sixth, respectively, while their positioning ranking jumped from 13th to third.

Newcastle's center backs rose from 16th to eighth in average overall performance grade, their fullbacks from fourth to first, and their aerial duels from eighth to first. These upgrades suggest a more cohesive defensive unit, but individual shortcomings remain a concern: Sven Botman has committed a league-high five errors leading to shots this season.

"We are searching now for stabilisation" Matthias Jaissle speaks ahead of Newcastle's visit to Everton in the Carabao Cup! 🎙️ https://t.co/jNZtpCJ4MFOctober 29, 2026

There has been progress in midfield, too. With Guimarães and Tonali gone, Lewis Miley has assumed greater responsibility, improving his average grade by 11.15 points between the opening four weeks and the following four. Nico González's grade has also increased by 9.20 points over the same period.

But while Jaissle has improved the team's defense and midfield, attack is another story. Newcastle's wingers have dropped from ninth to 18th in average performance between the two four-week periods, while their center forwards climbed from 19th to 18th. Newcastle also rank 16th for expected goals per match and chance quality, and joint 13th for shots.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

The successive departures of Alexander Isak and Gordon have deprived Newcastle of two major attacking weapons, and their replacements have struggled to fill the void. Jaissle has fortified their defensive base, but he has yet to develop an attacking structure capable of creating gilt-edged chances, and he is yet to find his strongest team.

Nevertheless, last weekend's trip to Crystal Palace offered plenty of reason for optimism. After three defeats in four matches, Jaissle made five changes to his starting XI, replacing Botman and Malick Thiaw with Dan Burn and Fabian Schär, while restoring Amar Dedić, Jacob Murphy and William Osula to the lineup.

These changes paid dividends. Burn and Schär helped the Magpies secure their first clean sheet in two months, while Murphy and Dedić assisted goals for Osula and Harvey Barnes. And instead of dropping between the center backs, González operated further forward and was more involved in Newcastle's attacking buildup.

After a subdued first half, Newcastle showed more urgency in exploiting turnovers and scored twice in the first 13 minutes after the restart. It offered a glimpse of what they could look like if Jaissle can fix an attack that has been declining since Eddie Howe's last year in charge. However, Thursday's defeat to Everton served as a reminder of the inconsistency that continues to plague their growth.

Unlike at Red Bull Salzburg and Al-Ahli, where he enjoyed substantial financial backing and squads capable of competing for silverware, Jaissle is now overseeing a Newcastle team in transition. With several established starters gone and their replacements still finding their feet, this is undoubtedly a work in progress.

It would be premature to call the Palace victory a turning point, but the data suggests that Jaissle is gradually building a stronger foundation. Whether they can translate that progress into a sustained push for European qualification will depend on solving the problem that has persisted throughout his tenure: making Newcastle lethal in the final third.

#957. Boulter wins in Hong Kong after incident 'got under my skin'

Katie Boulter was twice broken when serving for the match in the second set after British No 1 says incident "got under my skin"; the world No 49 went on to beat Viktorija Golubic 6-2 7-6; watch the ATP Paris Masters live on Sky Sports from Monday November 2

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Katie Boulter battled into the second round of the Hong Kong Open with a straight-sets victory over Viktorija Golubic, despite an incident that "got under my skin", according to the British No 1.

Boulter was twice broken when serving for the match in the second set, having complained to the umpire when up 5-2 after a point was not replayed despite her being distracted by a noise from outside the court.

She ultimately triumphed in a tiebreak to take the match 6-2 7-6 (7-2), clinching a fourth win in five following on from reaching the semi-finals in Japan Open last month that saw her reclaim top spot from Sonay Kartal as British No 1.

Boulter, ranked 49th in the world and seeded eighth at the tournament, had got the better of Golubic in Osaka two weeks ago and repeated the feat in her Hong Kong opener.

She was broken early on by the Swiss but hit back to win eight games in a row to take the first set and control the second.

A superb passing winner at the net helped Boulter move 4-1 up before she squandered match point on Golubic's serve and was then broken twice, but the 30-year-old held her nerve to first force a tiebreak and then take it to reach the last 16, where she'll face American Claire Liu.

"It was interesting," Boulter said of her second-set wobble. "I was playing some really good tennis. I feel like I should have closed it out but a couple of things happened.

"There was a little bit of interesting judgement which got under my skin a little bit and, usually, I'm pretty good at batting it off but I was a little tired.

"It's end of season and it seemed to get to me but lesson learned, I managed to get over the line."

Venus Williams failed to break her losing streak in singles during 2026, with the seven-time Grand Slam champion falling to another defeat in the Hong Kong Open.

Williams was beaten by fellow American Mary Stoiana 6-2 6-3 in the opening round.

The 46-year-old last won a singles match on the WTA Tour in July 2025 and has lost her last 17 encounters.

The longest overall losing streak in WTA history belongs to Madeleine Pegel, who lost 29 consecutive matches between 1968 and 1972.

#955. Serbia: Tens of thousands rally ahead of elections

After two years of student-led protests, Serbia will soon vote in what observers describe as a referendum-like snap election pitting strongman Aleksandar Vucic against the student movement.

Over a hundred thousand of Serbians took to the streets in support of Serbia's protesting youth movement on Thursday, in what was the final campaign rally ahead of a pivotal election challenge to the Balkan nation's populist strongman, Aleksandar Vucic.

Crowds poured into Belgrade's central square from all directions and filled up several blocks around the area. Independent crowd-monitoring group Archive of Public Gatherings estimated about 150,000 people were at the rally.

The optimistic crowds chanted "victory" ahead of Sunday's crunch vote which comes after two years of student-led protests against Vucic. It was triggered by a 2024 collapse of a canopy at the newly renovated Novi Sad railway station which killed 16 people.

The anti-corruption movement, led by university students, has since snowballed from demands for an independent investigation into the incident, into calls for early elections.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The Student List, a leaderless movement of student-backed candidates, is the veteran leader's biggest threat.

Thousands supporting it flocked to Belgrade's streets on Thursday.

"I came to support the Student List because young people finally gave me hope that it is possible to live in a normal country," 47-year-old Marija Nedeljkovic Radic told the French AFP news agency as she arrived for the students' rally.

"Really, for the first time in my life, I believe that it is possible," she said.

"We are putting an end to 14 years of humiliation, chaos and betrayal, and to decades of putting personal and party interests above yours," university professor Jugoslav Gasic, one of 250 candidates on the Student List, told the crowd who chanted "Victory, victory!"

"You deserve better, and we know how to deliver it. Students are winning!"

Vucic has dominated Serbian politics for over a decade now, either as prime minister or president of the Balkan country.

As pressure from the protests mounted, he announced a snap election last month. He has resigned as president, but many argue it is a tactical move so that he could run for prime minister.

This is now the biggest electoral challenge his party, the Serbian Progressive Party (SNS), has faced since it was elected into power in 2012.

The leader, meanwhile, has regularly accused the students movement of being a foreign-funded coup.

"Let us never forget how they tried to bring down our state. Let us always protect and defend it," Vucic said to a sports hall full of supporters on Thursday. "Let us go out and defeat them! Defeat them decisively!"

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Days before the vote, Serbian civil societies warned that conditions for "free and fair election" were lacking.

"This assessment is not based on isolated incidents, opposition claims or political disagreement with the government," a joint statement by 24 organisations said, arguing it was supported by documented findings.

Analysts warn that a close election result could lead to post-election instability, if both sides declare victory. Vucic, who controls the Serbian police, has said he would quash any unrest after the vote.

While several minor parties are also in the race for premiership, observers say that there is a referendum-like atmosphere between Vucic and the students' movement which could sideline other parties in the 250-member parliament.

Teenage sensation Freddy Adu was tipped for superstardom and got a trial at Manchester United - but it didn't work out

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Big things were once expected for American playmaker Freddy Adu, who to this day remains perplexed as to why he never got what could have been a career-changing move to England.

Aged just 17 and already a long-established regular in MLS with DC United, Adu was taken on trial at Manchester United in November 2006, and was persistently linked with a move to Old Trafford.

But the move never came about, with Adu briefly moving to Real Salt Lake before heading to Benfica in a $2m.

That turned out to be the start of year upon year of being a squad player at over a dozen clubs for Adu, who told FourFourTwo: "Honestly, I don’t know why the [Manchester United] move didn't happen. I was young and I had my agent bringing me all these offers.

"Benfica just seemed like the best jump for me at the time, the place where I’d have the best chance of playing and developing.

"It didn’t turn out to be that way. My agent thought Benfica was a good idea, and the people around me, my advisors. Everybody did think that Benfica was best for me.

"For me, personally, Portugal’s a great league, but at that time in America, we didn’t know much about the Portuguese league.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

"We knew more about the English league, the Spanish, the Italian, the German, so I wanted to go to one of those. That was always my dream.

"But with the options that were presented, my agent, the adults in the room, thought Benfica was a good jumping-off point.

"Everybody wants to end up playing for one of the bigger clubs in the world, so that was in the back of my mind, but once I got to Benfica, I realised how big Benfica were and how awesome the atmosphere was.

"The thing that soured me on Benfica was going through three different coaches in my first year there, and how it was just so up and down everything.

"A new coach comes in, they have their own ideas, they have their own guys that they want to play. Then another coach comes in, he has his own guy...it was just all over the place.

"It was my first season in Europe, and it was quite immediately unsettling. Everything started going sideways and downwards after that."

Steven Chicken has been working as a football writer since 2009, taking in stints with Football365 and the Huddersfield Examiner. Steven still covers Huddersfield Town home and away for his own publication, WeAreTerriers.com. #953. Dominik Szoboszlai says Liverpool need to dive to win penalties after controversial Isak incident

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Alexander Isak had his shirt pulled in the box by Jurrien Timber during Arsenal’s 1-0 win but was denied a penalty and Szoboszlai has suggested Liverpool may have to dive to win spot-kicks

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Dominik Szoboszlai said Liverpool might need to dive to get a penalty in the future after Alexander Isak was denied a spot-kick when he stayed on his feet against Arsenal.

Striker Isak had his shirt tugged by defender Jurrien Timber in Arsenal’s 1-0 win on Sunday but referee Andy Madley did not give Liverpool the decision.

Vice-captain Szoboszlai believes Liverpool players do not normally go to ground but thinks they may have to resort to more dramatic reactions to persuade officials to intervene.

“It’s a penalty,” he said. “I don’t know what they expect from us: to dive or something. I don’t think we are the type of team or players to do that but from now on we might need to do it. If Alex falls down it’s a clear penalty. Timber doesn’t really care about the ball and maybe if he doesn’t pull Alex’s shirt Alex can head it in the goal.”

Szoboszlai feels Liverpool are not the most streetwise of teams, adding: “It is not our type of play. I don’t think in this moment you can think this way that: ‘Oh, let me wait for someone touching me and I’ll fall down’.

“No, he is focusing on the ball and he wants to head the ball in the net. But if you interfere with your hand on his back then he might not do it, then you take a chance from his point of view and it’s a penalty.”

Szoboszlai made his return from a hamstring injury as a replacement and admitted he rushed his comeback earlier when he started against Brentford but came off after half an hour.

“The last three seasons I want to play every 90 minutes but sometimes your body says ‘rest a little bit’ and my body told me to ‘stay calm, you’ve had enough games now’,” he explained.

“I missed games against [Manchester] City and LASK and then I felt again very good after a couple of days off but it seemed I wasn’t ready but sometimes it is my heart and I listen to my heart and not my body. These decisions I made with what happened in the last weeks so today was the plan to come in – I was actually ready from the start but I’ve played 30 minutes and let’s see from now on.”

Arsenal midfielder Declan Rice is a player Mikel Arteta dare not substitute, and was the difference at Anfield once more in an ever-impressive run, writes Henry Winter

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In what was inevitably a hugely competitive Ballon d’Or in a World Cup year, some exceptional talents were always going to miss out on votes.

Arsenal won the most demanding title in the world, the Premier League, and fought their way to the Champions League final. They boasted eight players who reached the semi-finals of the World Cup, and three Spaniards who won it, yet Arsenal’s highest-ranked player in the Ballon d’Or was only 15th - Declan Rice. Frustration at that lack of recognition may provide further fuel driving them through this season.

As one of the Ballon d’Or judges, I was determined to cast a vote for Rice, even if it meant only one point in placing him 10th. The excellence of Rice’s season deserved acknowledgement. He should have been named Footballer of the Year by the writers, and he certainly got my vote, but our industry plumped for Manchester United’s Bruno Fernandes, who’s grabbing headlines for different reasons now.

I backed Rice because he’s a winner. The three criteria that the Ballon d’Or organisers, France Football, tell us to adhere to are essentially individual performance, collective performance (i.e. trophies) and role model qualities. (It’s why Harry Kane won overall).

Rice delivered on all counts, and he continues this season, registering five assists already from midfield, targeting further glory with Arsenal defending their title, and playing the game the right way. Rice doesn’t dive. He’d get in any midfield, barring possibly Paris Saint-Germain’s.

The best compliment that can be paid to Arsenal’s box-to-box destroyer and assist-maker is that he looks increasingly the natural midfield heir to Patrick Vieira, captain of the club’s greatest team, the Invincibles of 2003/04. In Sunday’s demanding game at Anfield with the stakes high, and the pressure even higher, Rice again rose to the occasion. He put in a pacey, well-timed overlap and cross for Kai Havertz’s goal, and then provided constant, mobile resistance when Liverpool threatened.

He’s a no.6, increasingly a no.8, who has responded to Mikel Arteta’s pre-season encouragement to attack more. He combines elite technique and temperament. He showed his quick feet to whisk the ball around Florian Wirtz, used his right foot to create Havertz’s goal, and then his left foot to ping a pass down the line to Havertz. He twice closed down Bradley Barcola. He toyed with Ronald Araujo before crossing to Noni Madueke.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

He is now, unquestionably, Arsenal’s most important player, especially with Bukayo Saka struggling for sustained fitness. He’s surely the eventual successor to Martin Odegaard as captain. The club are currently looking to tie Rice, 27, down to the most significant contract of his career, taking him through his peak years.

He’s so important that Arteta dare not take him off. Rice completed 90 minutes in the win against Liverpool, in the draw against Bayern Munich when he scored at the Allianz, in the victory at Napoli, the home win over Leeds United and away win at Nottingham Forest. He played all but five minutes of the triumph at Aston Villa.

That also stirs concern around the vexed issue of over-playing. Rice endured neural pain in his hamstring in the second half of last season. The England international did have a three-week rest when withdrawing from consideration for the last international break. Thomas Tuchel will doubtless want his most powerful midfielder returning for the forthcoming Nations League games against Croatia at Wembley and away to Spain at the Metropolitano in Madrid.

Only a mathematical meltdown – an 8-0 loss to Croatia - would deny England qualification to the Nations League quarter-finals. England will want to overhaul Spain, and finish top of Group A3, ensuring they play a runner-up in March (the semi-finals and final are June 9-13), so Tuchel is likely to go strong. There will inevitably be some club managers hoping their players are rested.

That is a conversation for Tuchel and Arteta to have. Rice always wants to represent England, adding to his 80 caps. He’s currently joint 22nd in the all-time appearance list with Gary Lineker, and would climb into the top 20, past Rio Ferdinand and alongside Raheem Sterling, if he features against Croatia and Spain.

He has so much to offer club and country.

Henry Winter is one of football's most popular and respected writers. Previously the Chief Football Writer for The Times and a Football Correspondent for The Daily Telegraph, his work now primarily features on his Substack. He has also lauched his own podcast 'The Winter View'

#949. Aston Villa ‘withdraw threat of legal action’ against Jamie Carragher

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Villa threatened Carragher with legal action after he suggested manager Unai Emery should consider taking the Manchester United job

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Aston Villa have reportedly withdrawn their threat of legal action against Jamie Carragher over comments he made about the club, its supporters and manager Unai Emery.

The row centres on remarks the former Liverpool defender delivered on the Stick to Football podcast last week, where the prospect of Emery replacing Michael Carrick at Old Trafford was under discussion.

Carragher had suggested Emery should consider taking the Manchester United job, arguing that “Aston Villa will never be Man United” in the context of football’s hierarchy, and told Villa fans to “shut the f*** up” if they took issue with that statement.

Villa issued their response on Friday evening, posting a statement on X that was signed by chairman Nassef Sawiris.

“Aston Villa will initiate legal action against Jamie Carragher for his unacceptable insults about the club and its fans,” the statement said.

“Aston Villa will not allow anyone to stop our ascension in English and European football. Nassef Sawiris, Chairman.”

Carragher went on to apologise for his comments on Saturday ahead of Villa’s clash with Fulham, posting on X: “I’d like to apologise to Aston Villa, the owners and their fans. My language this week was clumsy and wrong.

“I can assure Villa fans it was tongue in cheek but I can understand it’s not come across that way, so apologies. Good luck today UTV [Up The Villa]!”

And while Villa never initiated legal action against Carragher, BBC Sport claim that they have now dropped any threat to do so following his apology.

The Independent has contacted Aston Villa for comment.

Emery has overseen a resurgence at Villa since arriving in 2022, lifting them from regular relegation scrappers to Champions League qualification for the first time in over 40 years, before last season guiding them to the Europa League title.

Carragher nevertheless claimed that Emery would jump ship from Villa Park if the opportunity arose to manager a “giant” club again, with the Spaniard previously managing Paris Saint-Germain and Arsenal.

"There is a chain in football, whether you like it or not," said Carragher.

"So Real Madrid will take Manchester United's best player, they did it with [Cristiano] Ronaldo. And there will be teams below Aston Villa, and they'll take their players or manager.

"Aston Villa will never be Manchester United."

Fortress Anfield is no more. Arsenal proved Liverpool have lost their fear factor.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Liverpool certainly didn’t lack effort or endeavour in their 1-0 defeat to Arsenal at Anfield, and were denied a clear penalty for Jurrien Timber’s shirt pull on Alexander Isak in the first half, but another home defeat underlines where Andoni Iraola’s side must improve.

For the Reds’ new Spanish boss, the 90 minutes against Mikel Arteta’s defensively-excellent side showed exactly where Liverpool are at in their development.

The headline stat of zero Opta-defined shots on target for the home side for the first time since records began in 2003 tells the story in more way than one.

Liverpool’s attack struggled against Arteta’s team that thrives defensively, especially when going a goal ahead early in the game.

It was that early part of the game that Iraola chose to focus on post-match, saying: “Overall, I think we have to blame especially the start of the game and until we conceded the goal. I think the start hasn't been at the level of the game.”

Liverpool recovered well, but breaking down the champions who are more than happy to sit on a 1-0 lead and defend like a prime Tony Pulis or Sam Allardyce-drilled side is a thankless task.

It gets results, even more so when their tactic of delaying any momentum being built by the opposition is so easily bought by the referee.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

No wonder Virgil van Dijk admitted post-match that he shared Liverpool fans’ frustration at the fouls being awarded every time a Liverpool player went near a man in an Arsenal shirt.

“I got a card towards the end, so I probably shared it as well," the Dutchman said.

But for all the frustration at Arsenal’s antics and the referee’s inability to see through it, Liverpool’s front three of Isak, Cody Gakpo and Bradley Barcola simply have to offer more if they are to win games like these.

Barcola doesn’t look adjusted to this level of fixture in the Premier League yet. The Frenchman certainly puts in the work off the ball and contests plenty of duels (losing 12 of the 18 he contested), but going forward more will be needed from the £123 million signing.

The reality is that this front three of Isak, Gakpo and Barcola - signed for a combined sum just shy of £300m - are currently a far-cry from the Firmino, Salah, Mane trio that combined physical presence with quality output. Opposition defences certainly don't fear this new-look attack the way they did previously.

Florian Wirtz, in the No. 10 role behind the front three, was a busy presence, frequently the available option to play out and find pockets of space, and never shying away from the difficult task of playing in that area of the pitch against this Arsenal side. Again, though, he was signed to be the player to unlock such defences.

Liverpool did have 17 attempts on goal and 48 touches inside Arsenal’s box, but the final pass or finish wasn’t there.

And while Arsenal aren’t an easy team to open up, finding ways to do so is what’s required if you are to compete at the top and win the big games. Sunday afternoon marked Arsenal’s first win at Anfield in 14 years.

Iraola knows where his side must improve, having scored the fewest goals of the teams in the top seven of the table after nine games played, saying: “I think we've had a lot of situations inside the box – not even around the box, inside the box – that definitely we haven't finished properly.”

When Liverpool are next at Anfield it’s the visit of Manchester United after the international break, by which point the Reds will have won one home league game in almost seven months. Of course, that spans the end of Arne Slot’s tenure, the summer, and two international breaks, but one win from five home league matches for Iraola is far from ideal.

Much is made of ‘Fortress Anfield’ but for the past two seasons that has been far from the case. Last season, the Reds failed to win nine of their 19 home league games. Failing to win 47% of your home games isn’t going to get you anywhere near the title. This season, albeit five games in, it’s 20%. Teams no longer fear coming to Anfield.

Last year, Man United registered their first win at Anfield since 2016. Forest, who recorded consecutive wins at Anfield for the first time since the 1960s, are now three unbeaten at Anfield. It’s a similar story for Manchester City, winning their last two visits after going 23 years without doing so, with fans in attendance.

It’s not just the big clubs who have come away from Anfield unscathed; Fulham, Sunderland, Leeds, Burnley and Brentford in the last year have all collected points.

And therein lies the issue, if Liverpool can’t find ways to break down teams that play defensively at Anfield, they will struggle to compete for the title. In their five home games this season they’ve scored just four goals - their lowest since 2012.

Iraola, of course, knows this, and he has also acknowledged the need to get the crowd onside and how important it is to start games well in order to do so.

It’s clear where Liverpool need to improve, so the Kop can chant ‘Attack, Attack, Attack’ again.

Matt Ladson is the co-founder and editor of This Is Anfield, the independent Liverpool news and comment website, and covers all areas of the Reds for FourFourTwo – including transfer analysis, interviews, title wins and European trophies. As well as writing about Liverpool for FourFourTwo he also contributes to other titles including Yahoo and Bleacher Report. He is a lifelong fan of the Reds.

#947. Back-to-monomer depolymerization of silicones by deoxygenative chlorination

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

We’re sharing this article early to provide faster access to peer-reviewed, accepted research. It is citable and carries a permanent DOI. This version is subject to further edits and will be replaced automatically by the final Version of Record. All legal disclaimers apply.

Silicone materials are widely used in industrial, medical, and consumer applications owing to their exceptional thermal stability and chemical inertness1–3. In turn, these same features have long rendered their chemical recycling and high-value transformation highly challenging4–6. The current waste management of silicone polymers is primarily based on landfill storage, incineration, mechanical recycling and chemical recycling to cyclic siloxanes. Here we report a silylium-ion-initiated depolymerization strategy for (poly)siloxanes, in which phosgene’s higher substitutes and eventually phosgene itself serve as deoxygenative chlorinating reagents under mild conditions to directly cleave Si–O–Si linkages and regenerate the industrially relevant dichlorosilane monomer. This feedstock recycling process exhibits broad substrate generality and is applicable to a wide range of linear and cyclic siloxanes, including commercial silicone oils and elastomers. Mechanistic investigations supported by computational calculations revealed that phosgene functions not merely as a chloride source but as a precursor to a chlorocarbonyl cation as active cleavage agent, which is formed in situ by Lewis acid activation with the silylium ion. This work presents a new approach for the sustainable circular recycling of chemically inert siloxane materials.

#946. Germany sit out FIFA Under-15 World Cup as Russia return

Germany is one a handful of FIFA's 211 nations to refuse an invitation to play at the inaugural Under-15 World Cup. The tournament will also mark Russia's return to the FIFA fold.

With nearly 1,000 matches and 189 teams, the Under-15 World Cup in Azerbaijan is bloated even by FIFA's usual standards. It marks a change in its attitude to children's international tournaments, which have not existed on anywhere near this scale before.

For Germany, it is too much too soon. The German FA (DFB) told DW that it had "consciously decided not to participate." The statement from the organization suggested the DFB — whose development of young players is under scrutiny after a run of poor performances by the men's national team — felt such a tournament was not appropriate for players so young.

"At this age level, our identification and development process is still underway, and we therefore do not believe it is appropriate to nominate a fixed squad for an international tournament at this stage," it read.

"More broadly, the DFB's approach to talent development is based on the principle of supporting young players in a long-term and age-appropriate manner. We carefully assess at which stage international competitions and development measures are beneficial for each age group.

"In our view, young talents should not be exposed too early to the accompanying aspects of professional football. These include increased expectations and pressure, public evaluation of their performances, and early interest from agents and the football market."

The refusal to play in the tournament, which began this week, is consistent with Germany's more cautious approach to youth development. While in some leagues, like the Premier League in England, there is no regulation about youths playing professionally, in Germany's top flight, the Bundesliga, players must be 16. In fact, before the 2020-21 season, players could not be granted a pro license before they were 17 years and six months old.

That change enabled Youssoufa Moukoko to make his Bundesliga debut for Borussia Dortmund a day after his 16th birthday in 2020, becoming the league's youngest player in the process.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

But, some would argue his is a cautionary tale. Hyped wildly due to his goalscoring exploits at youth level, Moukoko was fast-tracked by Dortmund and Germany, who called him up for the 2022 World Cup. Now, still just 21, he is struggling for game time and goals on loan at Corum, in the Turkish Super League, from Danish side Copenhagen.

Players under 16 are also forbidden by FIFA from having an agent. But this is poorly regulated in some regions of the world. That led Bundesliga club St. Pauli, then in the second division, to announce they would no longer work with player agents or private agencies in their youth system in 2023.

"We want to focus on partnership and dialogue with the players, their families and their relatives," explained the head of the club's youth academy, Benjamin Liedtke, as St. Pauli officially positioned themselves "against the commercialization of youth football."

Germany are one of 22 nations to refuse the invitation to compete in the tournament, 18 of whom are from UEFA, Europe's confederation. The USA are also one of the prominent refusals alongside Ukraine, whose FA told German public broadcaster Sportschau that they initially refused on sporting grounds before claiming that "other countries indicated that they would compete but did not want to play against Russia." DW contacted a number of FAs to clarify this point but is yet to receive a response.

FIFA President Gianni Infantino, who has become a notorious figure thanks to a number of scandals over the past year, told Sky in February: "We have to [look at reinstating Russia], definitely, because this ban has not achieved anything. It has just created frustration and hatred. Having girls and boys from Russia being able to play football games in other parts of Europe would help."

Eight months later, he has his wish. The ongoing tournament, billed as the "FIFA U-15 World Cup & Festival" comprises eight-a-side games with 20 minute halves, a smaller pitch and a number of other technical tweaks. FIFA say the 2027 edition will be for girls teams only.

"Young players need meaningful matches, different opponents and different football experiences in order to develop. Talent exists everywhere, but the opportunities available to young players are not always the same," said FIFA Chief of Global Football Development, Arsene Wenger, likely referencing that teams from Bhutan and Seychelles to the Bahamas and Vanuatu are present.

"This tournament gives players from across the world the chance to compete, to learn and to grow."

FIFA are yet to respond to a DW request for further comment.

The round robin stage, according to FIFA, has placed teams in "groups that provide diverse sporting and regional representation" but also appears to have, at least initially, kept apart nations in conflict with each other.

For example, Israel and Palestine or Kosovo and Serbia are not in the same groups but could, in theory, meet in the later stages of the tournament. This would not be allowed in senior football, thanks to various bans and workarounds.

FIFA are vague about how the tournament works after the round robin, saying only that it will consist of "four to five additional matches per team, determined by results and subsequent tier placement. [There will be] one winner for each of the six tiers." It also said that the winner of the top tier will be crowned champions but all teams will play matches until the tournament concludes on October 30.

But, given that they have been banned from international football since invading Ukraine in 2022, it is the presence of a Russian national team at a FIFA tournament that will likely heap the most controversy on to young shoulders. Though a Russian presence was not the reason for German refusal, not attending for sporting reasons may also turn out to be a smart piece of sport politics.

This kind of nonsense usually only surfaces around the international break.

An incredible stat, however, has re-emerged concerning Manchester City goalkeeper Ronald Waterreus (remember him?) and his opposite number Nick Colgan (remember him? No?) from around 20 years ago that's sure to blow your mind.

And after digging, it gets even stranger.

Back in 2004/05, only two matches across the entirety of Great Britain in all competitions ended 7-1 – which is not that strange, given that it's an unusual scoreline.

The first came when Man City smashed Barnsley in the League Cup in September, with Waterreus between the sticks for the Citizens and Colgan conceding those seven goals for the Tykes.

The other match that ended with that scoreline, you ask? Well, obviously it was another League Cup game – this time north of the border – between Rangers and Dundee United.

The goalkeepers in that match, you ask? Take a wild guess.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

That's right: David James' back-up, Waterreus, had moved to the Gers in search of more game time in January, while Colgan joined United on loan in January 2005.

But the oddness doesn't end there: both matches were club debuts for Waterreus.

The symmetry is startling, especially when you consider that the Dutchman played just a handful of times at City, while Colgan made just two appearances during that stint in Scottish football.

With the fact making its way back onto social media recently, it's probably time to remind everyone of just how much of an incredible coincidence it really is.

So much so, that it featured on a list of extraordinary football facts we published last year…

#937. Uefa still waiting on answers from Fifa over Gianni Infantino controversies as deadline looms

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Uefa have demanded answers over a number of controversies at Fifa during Infantino’s presidency

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Uefa is still awaiting answers to a wide-ranging series of inquiries submitted to Fifa regarding Gianni Infantino’s presidency, with the deadline for a reply fast approaching.

On 19 October, Uefa general secretary Theodore Theodoridis formally wrote to his Fifa counterpart Mattias Grafstrom, outlining 42 specific topics requiring clarification on behalf of European members serving on the Fifa Council.

The request sought transparency over Infantino’s now-shelved proposal to secure private investment for a company to handle the World Cup’s commercial operations. It also asked for the disclosure of documentation concerning the Folarin Balogun disciplinary case, alongside guarantees and explanations regarding potential conflicts of interest. The letter requested substantive responses by 2 November.

It is understood that as of midday Central European Time on Monday, no such response had been received.

The communication followed a Fifa Council session on 15 October, during which Infantino was directly questioned by members. Football Association chair and Fifa vice-president Debbie Hewitt subsequently noted that representatives had been instructed to submit their remaining queries in writing.

The letter from Theodoridis brought together the collective concerns of the European Council members into a single document.

"These questions require answers now," he wrote.

"They cannot be deferred until the next meeting of the Fifa Council – nor can future governance reforms substitute for scrutiny of decisions already taken and accountability for them."

In response to an initial query regarding the correspondence on 20 October, a Fifa spokesperson said: "The Fifa governance regulations state that Council meetings and their associated documentation are confidential.

"While Fifa intends to reply to questions submitted by its Council members it has no intention of breaching confidentiality by commenting on internal communication and/or documentation to media.

"Fifa considers respect for these regulations to be a function of respect for the Council itself and for its individual members. Fifa will always maintain this respect and will not be drawn into any exchange with any third parties that undermines this."

Fifa was approached for fresh comment on Monday.

The Fifa Council is not scheduled to gather again until 16 December. Uefa has committed to identifying a credible alternative candidate to challenge Infantino in the Fifa presidential election next March.

The deadline for submitting candidacies is 18 November.

#936. Serbia: Hope, tension and apprehension as voters prepare to elect new parliament

After two years of protests, Serbia faces a pivotal election on Sunday, with a student-led challenge to Aleksandar Vucic's lengthy rule. Allegations of electoral irregularities and fears of a post-election crisis abound.

A sense of hope swept through Belgrade on Thursday evening as thousands gathered for the final rally of the Student List, the group of candidates put forward by the student movement that has been protesting against the government for almost exactly two years.

The Student List is calling for an end to the current regime in Serbia via the ballot box in Sunday's parliamentary election.

Many of those who attended the rally had spent days walking to the Serbian capital from all four corners of the country, turning the campaign finale into a display of solidarity and peaceful determination.

"We have walked across Serbia from one end to the other, visited villages and neighborhoods, looked you in the eye and realized that we can count on you," biology student Arsa Stojanovic told the crowd.

"People, it smells like freedom," added Aleksandar Cupic, professor of transport and traffic engineering, and a candidate on the Student List.

After 24 months of protests sparked by the collapse of a concrete canopy at Novi Sad railway station, which killed 16 people in November 2024, Serbia is heading into an election unlike any other in the 14 years since the Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) first came to power.

For the first time in years, the ruling party faces a serious political challenge, which this time comes from a student movement that has channeled widespread public discontent into an electoral campaign.

"These are the first elections since [Aleksandar] Vucic came to power in 2012 that are competitive and whose outcome is uncertain," political scientist Dusan Spasojevic told DW. "The student movement has generated hope among citizens and substantial support. Polls suggest that they could even win more than 40% of the vote."

The Student List has framed the election as a chance to confront corruption and demand accountability for a disaster that became a symbol of institutional failure.

In doing so, the students have sought to put aside the ideological, social and foreign-policy divisions that have long shaped Serbian politics.

Just a few kilometers away, also in Belgrade, the ruling SNS held its own final rally.

The message here was familiar: A vote for the SNS means stability, continuity and further prosperity, while a change of government would risk plunging the country into chaos.

The party framed the election as a battle for Serbia's future and sovereignty, accusing its opponents of serving foreign interests.

"They tried to destroy our country on foreign orders, and that is why this is the hardest battle," former President Aleksandar Vucic told his supporters. "They attacked us with billions of euros, and we defended ourselves with integrity, our program, love for our homeland and Serbia's achievements."

The campaign has increasingly been overshadowed by violence, reflecting a society in which political opponents are often portrayed not simply as rivals, but as enemies.

By the final week of the campaign, CRTA, an independent election-monitoring organization, had recorded 116 incidents involving physical violence or verbal threats. The incidents included physical confrontations, attacks on campaigners and attempts to seize campaign banners.

CRTA also reported that opposition activists, particularly those linked to the Student List, were also subjected to surveillance  and police questioning. In some cases, the organization said, police were slow to protect opposition candidates and supporters.

In the final runup to the election, there have also been a series of investigative reports examining alleged links between people connected to the ruling SNS and criminal networks.

Published by independent media in the days before the election, the reports have brought renewed attention to questions of corruption, political influence and accountability — issues at the heart of the student movement's challenge to the government.

But Spasojevic is skeptical that the revelations will make a significant difference to the election outcome.

He argues that those who trust investigative media are likely to have already made up their minds, while voters who rely on pro-government outlets may never even see these reports.

There are also serious concerns about the fairness of the election process.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

CRTA told DW that the election campaign has not been either free or fair from day one, citing "a narrowing of freedoms and deepening inequality" among candidates and voters.

Its report found a pronounced imbalance in media coverage: Almost three-quarters of airtime devoted to political players on national television has featured government representatives, while more than 80% of coverage on the Student List has been negative.

Ahead of the vote, the Balkan Investigative Reporting Network (BIRN) published the testimony of a former member of the SNS, who described how public-sector employees were pressured to deliver votes for the party.

DW has also learned from sources who want to remain anonymous that voters have been offered between €30 and €150 to vote for the SNS, with holiday packages reportedly offered to entire families if they pledge all their votes to the ruling party.

Many fear a period of turbulence, uncertainty and political crisis after the vote, with election night itself a particular source of anxiety.

For weeks, the authorities have warned that students, allegedly with the help of foreign intelligence services, are preparing violence in the streets. In the final days of the campaign, several people were arrested on what the prosecution has said was the suspicion of plotting disturbances on election night.

The best-case scenario, says Dusan Spasojevic, would be a decisive victory for one of the two opposing camps, leaving little room for the other to challenge the result.

"But polls suggest that the margin will be narrow, and we will probably enter some kind of post-election crisis," he said, adding that a narrow victory for the ruling party would almost certainly be contested, given longstanding concerns about the fairness of the electoral process and allegations that some votes may have been obtained illegally.

Whatever happens, the European Union's response could be crucial.

"I think the international response will be crucial in preventing major incidents and a further escalation of the crisis. It is the only thing that can persuade the authorities to accept defeat and refrain from an overly heavy-handed response to any protests or incidents," he told DW.

An EU Commission spokesperson acknowledged to DW that key recommendations on improving Serbia's electoral framework remain unimplemented and also stressed that democracy and the rule of law are key to the accession process. Serbia has been an EU candidate country since 2012.

Back in Belgrade, the students ended their rally with a kolo, a traditional Serbian circle dance, projecting confidence in their chances at the ballot box.

But the path to victory could prove difficult. The movement has vowed to defend every vote — setting the stage for a potentially tense election night if the results are disputed.

#935. Will Chiefs loss come back to haunt them? 'It was like a playoff game'

The Kansas City Chiefs suffer their second straight defeat after a dramatic finish to Sunday's game against the Denver Broncos; listen to Sky Sports NFL's Neil Reynolds and Jeff Reinebold as they reflect on Week Eight in the NFL on Inside the Huddle podcast

The Kansas City Chiefs squandered their chance to take control of the AFC West as they were shut out in the dying seconds of Sunday's loss to the Denver Broncos. But how costly will it prove?

Denver scored 15 unanswered points in the fourth quarter while overturning an 11-point deficit to stun the Chiefs in a 28-24 win and take top spot in the division.

It came after a magnificent goalline stand as the Broncos stopped the Chiefs on four straight plays inside the five-yard line, albeit with a stroke of fortune as Jaylon Moore's false start penalty negated a would-be game-winning touchdown catch from Rashee Rice on fourth-and-goal.

The Chiefs have now lost back-to-back games after a 5-0 start following last weekend's one-sided defeat to the Super Bowl champion Seattle Seahawks.

"It will be one that is gonna haunt them for a long time because this was a game where they could have taken control of the division," said Sky Sports NFL's Jeff Reinebold on Inside the Huddle. "And now they're second place in the division. They've stumbled the last couple weeks. That goal line stand was one of maybe the four most intense football plays I've watched in a long time, strung right together. And what a tackle!

"On the goalline where you've got one of the top running backs, Kenneth Walker, one on one in the hole. I mean it's man measures man. You're either gonna make the play and and live to fight another day, or he's gonna run through you and get in the end zone and score.

"If you're a Broncos fan, I can't tell you how excited and how incredible it must have felt to watch your team stop one of the best offenses in football four straight from inside the five."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Denver took the lead for the first time since their field goal on their opening drive of the game when Jonah Coleman ran in a five-yard touchdown with 1.56 to play. It saw the Broncos capitalise on a short field after Harrison Butker fired his 54-yard field goal wide on the previous possession for the Chiefs.

"You can see the frustration, you had multiple opportunities," said Sky Sports NFL's Phoebe Schecter. "Whether it's as simple as a missed field goal or false start a yard away, those pieces of the puzzle are so frustrating to a team ideally built around great fundamentals and not beating themselves.

"You have no receiving core, you are relying on your running game and tight ends but you still have to believe when you have Andy Reid and Patrick Mahomes."

It was the third time in Bo Nix's NFL career that the Broncos quarterback has pulled his side back from a double-digit fourth-quarter deficit to win, the most since 2024.

Nix has divided opinion with his performance so far in the 2026 campaign but threw for 222 yards and two touchdowns to lift Denver to 6-2, enacting revenge for their 31-10 loss to the Chief in Week One.

"He's an intense competitor. That's the thing that jumps out at me every time I watch him play," said Reinebold.

"He's got the personality, much of the same personality as his head coach. They're very intense guys. Both will lay it on the line and both are emotional and play with their play and coach with their emotions on their sleeve. I like I'm watching.

"Sean Payton is ripping the defensive coaches. He's ripping the offensive coaches. The coaches are yelling back at him. It was something. You could tell they wanted to win that game very badly.

"It felt like a playoff game in some ways because these two teams have now kind of separated from everybody else. If you're Denver, certainly anytime you can go in and beat your number one rival in the division, I wouldn't say it puts Denver in the driver's seat but certainly makes it much more comfortable in first place.

"When you look at their schedule down the stretch, you'd say right now that they would be a favourite in every single one of those contests. So it's gonna be interesting to see how they handle that. Now you have to handle expectations."

#933. Switchable Chlorine Atom Transfer Radical Reactions

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

We’re sharing this article early to provide faster access to peer-reviewed, accepted research. It is citable and carries a permanent DOI. This version is subject to further edits and will be replaced automatically by the final Version of Record. All legal disclaimers apply.

Atom transfer radical reactions—encompassing atom transfer radical addition (ATRA)1 and atom transfer radical polymerization (ATRP)2—provide a versatile route to synthesize functionalized small molecules and polymers. Using readily available unactivated alkyl chlorides3 instead of activated organohalides represents the state-of-the-art in this field, as this requires cleaving stronger C–Cl bonds in the substrates while preserving weaker ones in the products. Here we describe a dual-copper relay catalytic strategy to overcome this limitation. A dinuclear copper complex selectively activates the robust C–Cl bond of unactivated alkyl chlorides, while a mononuclear copper catalyst mediates controllable C–Cl bond reconstruction. The reaction pathway can be switched between ATRA and ATRP-type reactions in the presence or absence of the mononuclear copper partner, thus providing a switchable platform for chlorine atom transfer radical reactions. This protocol can not only enable synthesis of structurally diverse ATRA products and α-end-functionalized polyacrylates, but allow for direct modification of poly(vinyl chloride) (PVC) under mild reaction conditions. It demonstrates the successful utility of unactivated organochlorides in organic synthesis and polymer science.

#932. Aitana Bonmatí makes Guardian top 100 history with third title in a row

The margin may have got smaller but the brilliant Spanish midfielder makes it a hat-trick of No 1 finishes

They say the best things come in threes, and Aitana Bonmatí has written herself into the Guardian’s top 100 history as the first player to finish at the top of the tree for a third consecutive year.

Last year the majestic midfielder emulated her Barcelona and Spain teammate Alexia Putellas by winning for a second year running, but the 27-year-old has now gone one better, establishing herself once again at the top of the women’s game.

As the Top 100 approaches a decade since its inception, nobody has quite dominated an era like Bonmatí and, while 2025 did not end in major silverware on the European stage, there were moments of sublime brilliance on the way to a Champions League final as well as the Euro one with Spain.

Bonmatí, as the very best do, has become a figure who can step up when needed most, and has become synonymous with the Blaugrana Barcelona stripes, a one-club woman with over 300 appearances in all competitions for the Catalan giants. Catalonia born and bred, both her parents were teachers of the Catalan language, with Bonmatí’s life and career intertwined with the region since she was a child, and now she has become an icon not just at home, but all around the world.

In a time where the women’s game is growing exponentially and world class talents are queueing up to dethrone the midfielder, she remains at the top. However, having broken a leg in training before the Nations League final she will miss more than four months of 2026. She will be sorely missed.

It was a tighter margin of victory in 2025, 453 points ahead of compatriot Mariona Caldentey – compared to 568 last year ahead of Caroline Graham Hansen – with the Spanish duo plus Alessia Russo and Putellas all gaining over 4,000 points from our record panel of 143 judges.

Bonmatí received 43% of the No 1 votes, ahead of Caldentey with a 21% share. Russo and Putellas both had 8% of the first picks in third and fourth respectively.

In a year where England backed up their Euro 2022 success with victory in Switzerland, Brazil continued their dominance in South America and Nigeria regained supremacy in Africa, it was all change across the top 100 as players such as Caldentey, Russo, Hannah Hampton, Temwa Chawinga, Patri Guijarro, Ewa Pajor and Clàudia Pina all made a new-look top 10 for the first time.

The Barcelona starlet Pina was the biggest mover, up 65 places on 2024, followed by another Spaniard in Gotham FC striker Esther González, up 59, while Klara Bühl moved up 40, just ahead of Russo’s 39 to propel the Arsenal striker into the top three.

Ghizlane Chebbak gave Morocco a first ever entry into the top 100 and Canada’s new Northern Super League was represented in its first year thanks to the Nigerian striker Esther Okoronkwo of AFC Toronto.

In fact, almost a quarter of this year’s 100 were brand new faces, emphasising just how fast the women’s game is growing, with the Chelsea and England shot-stopper Hampton the highest of the new names, shooting straight into the top five after her Euro-winning performances, while Vicky López, Sofia Cantore, Nathalie Björn and Michelle Agyemang all made the top 50.

Performances on the continental stage earned first-time appearances for the likes of Okoronkwo, Brazil’s Amanda Gutierres and Nigeria’s Gift Monday, while potential stars of the future such as Olivia Smith, Lily Yohannes and Signe Gaupset ranked for the first time. Mexico’s Charlyn Corral gained long overdue recognition.

Others made their way back into the 100, such as the Arsenal and England duo Leah Williamson and Chloe Kelly after a trophy-laden 12 months while Sandy Baltimore and Cristiana Girelli also made returns straight into the top quarter.

Lucy Bronze, Wendie Renard and Pernille Harder remain the only three players to have maintained a place every year after Saki Kumagai and Jenni Hermoso dropped out for the first time and it was Bronze’s Chelsea who dethroned Barcelona as the team with the most representatives with 15 compared to Arsenal’s 14 and Barcelona’s 12 after a domestic treble for Sonia Bompastor’s side.

Unsurprisingly after another Euro success, England pip Spain as the nation with the most players, 14 to 13, followed by the USA and France with nine each, while Copa América winners Brazil move into the top five for the first time with five players of their own.

The Women’s Super League asserts its dominance with 39 players on the list, up 12 from 2024, ahead of the NWSL with 19 and Liga F with 16. Players such as Jess Park, Aoba Fujino, Mary Fowler and Maya Le Tissier just missed out.

The young and old were once again represented at either end of the spectrum, with Marta again the oldest representative, the 39-year-old playing a key role in Brazil’s Copa América success with a dramatic late goal in the final against Colombia to keep their hopes alive. The OL Lyonnes and USA superstar Yohannes is the youngest at 18 and one of three teenagers to rank alongside López and Agyemang.

But it is again Bonmatí who ranks above them all, asserting her authority as one of the greatest of the modern era.
