#850. How can playing for Manchester City fit into Marc Guéhi’s moral universe? | Barney Ronay

Club’s predicament raises interesting questions about principles, both for individuals and the Premier League

I felt unbelievably ponderous. My head was made of Aztec stone. I realised I didn’t want to be with all these people. Somebody came at me, a huge individual in silver and blue. I fell at his feet and grabbed one shoe. I started untying the lace. He kicked away from me. I got up and walked off. I was exceedingly hungry.

Not my words. Also not the words of the Manchester City centre-back Marc Guéhi, despite what you were thinking there. This is instead a condensed quote from the mind of Gary Harkness, existentially curious college running-back and the narrator of Don DeLillo’s great American football novel End Zone.

This passage describes a moment where Gary plays a game having been urged by his friends to smoke pot beforehand to discover whether it improves his understanding of time and space, or just makes him want to lie down and untie someone’s laces. It marks a turning point for Gary. To this point football has been a comforting world. He sees clarity in its militaristic rituals, finds in sport “the illusion that order is possible”, hears hidden truths in the coaches’ shouted instructions. Button up. Get fetal. Get fetal. Get fetal. Run with reckless abandon.

Now the illusion has collapsed. Gary walks off the football field and begins instead to fixate on cold war fears and nuclear apocalypse. Death and political power have entered the chat.

Now, I’m not saying Marc Guéhi is Gary Harkness. You might be saying that. That’s your choice. But Guéhi has seemed a bit distracted in the last few weeks. Oddly for an agile and technically sound centre-back, he has seemed brittle and absent, vulnerable to being pressed.

There have been a couple of things said about City’s players in this regard. The first is that their minds might not be wholly on the game, that in the middle of a game against Croatia, for example, concerned only with manoeuvring through tiny pockets of space, Nico O’Reilly is also thinking: “Hmm, but how is it possible even by omission to honestly contravene rules E.3 and E.4 which state clearly that …oh. Wait, no. Oh dear.”

Football doesn’t work like this. The physical game is a place of total focus. But still, nothing is watertight. And this speaks to the second thing people have said, repeated like an absolute truth, that the players are entirely separate from all this. They cannot be questioned here, or indeed expected to ask questions of their own. The players are simply avatars, employees, free from any kind of agency. Players don’t have access to Google. They cannot make moral judgments. And yes, this may not be true of any other human in any other field. It may be the case that elite footballers are in fact unusually empowered, free to do whatever they want. But the consensus is clear. It is not a footballer’s business to have opinions on their employers, or what happens out of their line of vision.

This does help to avoid some tricky conundrums. Guéhi, for example, is a man of absolute public principle. Fair enough. I respect his willingness to resist popular pressure and personalise his support for the rainbow armband by writing things about Jesus on top of it. This is living your values. It’s free speech, figuring out your own moral universe. Doing so by following the absolute tenets of his religion. Go for it.

At the same time, Guéhi is playing for a club that has been convicted of cheating and lying. People are free to disagree with the rules. But if others are sticking to them, this amounts to deceit, stolen win bonuses, stolen glory. And the Bible is very clear on this. Thessalonians 4:6: “No one should transgress and defraud his brother.” Proverbs 20:17: “Bread gained by deceit is sweet to a man, but afterward his mouth will be full of gravel.” Now, I don’t believe these words to be divinely ordained. They’re great words. Totally dig the vibe. But Guéhi does believe these things to be an absolute instruction. How does this fit together in his head? How does that gravel (pending appeal) taste right now?

Again, fine if you can square it. It’s a personal journey. Park the apparent moral dilemma. See if your legal team can come up with a better final outcome. But things have changed in one significant way since the verdict dropped, an element that is now unchallenged, and which has been largely unremarked in the middle of the chaos. Understandably so. This stuff is gruelling. Everyone just wants to watch some football in the brief lull between legal rage events. But there are two points worth making in the interim. The second of which is an admission that affects many other things.

The first issue is: do you actually understand the basis of the Manchester City appeal? That evidence has seemingly been leaked. The irrefutable body of evidence, Body Of Evidence 2, the long-awaited tribunal-based Madonna erotic thriller vehicle, contains a vital detail: the additional money in City’s coffers, almost a billion, did not come from the owners, the Abu Dhabi United Group, which is owned, like City, by Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed al-Nahyan. This would be against the rules. It came instead from the Abu Dhabi government, which is essentially the Abu Dhabi royal family, of which Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed al-Nahyan is a member; as he is also, wearing a different hat, of the Abu Dhabi government.

And maybe this means it’s fine. It seems the government often tops up the sponsor companies like a benevolent uncle. In the period the charges relate to there was no need for sponsor deals to be of market value, as there is now. So if we accept all this, if we can establish a binding principle of wearing different hats in different rooms, this may be a way out. Maybe.

This is a familiar concept in the high court, in an age of shell companies and tricky fiscal flows. Mega-million cases hang on whether ownership really is separate, or whether this is, to echo a phrase, a sham process. The person on the Clapham omnibus might not buy any of this. Do these really seem like separate entities? Or a bit like adopting a French accent when the bailiffs ring up and maintaining that, no, Monsieur Ronay is not here, and he definitely doesn’t run this dry cleaners. That, instead, is me.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

If you make the case you win the case. This is all in the end about the application of rules, and that is a good thing. But the key point here is the secondary issue derived from this. City’s leaked defence, in making their case, is also saying, without pretence or mucking about, that the club is indeed funded by the Abu Dhabi government. This is something City’s fans have at times weirdly denied. But we have it in plain sight now, not just admitted but insisted on. The ultimate source of the dizzying success of the club that has defined a Premier League era is the government. Guéhi is, in effect, an Abu Dhabi civil servant. Perhaps the United Arab Emirates national team should have six stars on their jersey, one for each Premier League won. But there is no way of covering your ears now. City actively want us to accept this.

What are the consequences of this new fact? It comes with two urgent questions. The first is the moral one. Back again to Guéhi as the best example. This is what he is promoting here. And Guéhi is a man entirely guided by the principles of his faith. A private matter perhaps, except that it’s not, because Guéhi’s church explicitly orders its members to go out and proselytise. Guéhi is a member of Ballers in God, which actively tries to awaken Christian faith in the dressing room. He plays with Christian messages on his matchday kit intended to make you, the reader, think yes, maybe I too should follow this evangelical church.

And here is the key thing. This is a criminal offence in Abu Dhabi. Under UAE penal code, giving out Christian leaflets will get you arrested. A Christian pastor in the UAE was sentenced to a year in prison for giving a Muslim a Bible. Some Americans were deported for giving out Christian literature in the Dubai shopping district. Spreading the gospel, which Guéhi is morally bound to do, is illegal in the place that pays his direct employers.

Are players just avatars, empty shells? How much do you really believe in this? These are, more than ever, very interesting questions. And they don’t just apply to issues of personal principle.

The regulator now has this information, too. Abu Dhabi funded the purchase of Nolito. Abu Dhabi dictated the flow of English football finance. The same pocket that paid for this is also funding at arm’s length the civil war in Sudan, the hospital massacres, the piles of bodies so high they can be seen from satellite imaging. Abu Dhabi, which criminalises homosexuality, which crushes dissent, is openly identifying itself as the mega-funder of a Premier League club. Is this a fit and proper influence?

There are very obvious reasons why this is not desirable. Governments spy and wage war and break rules. They have a sacred trust to promote their own interests by any means necessary. It is hard to see how this kind of owner fits the regulatory framework. Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund had to twirl through semantic hoops when buying Newcastle to establish it was an entity at one remove from a government, as opposed to a government entity. In making the opposite case for their funding City have not only exposed their own live-your-values central defender, they have put themselves in a place where, even if you win on one front, you’ve started to look like a very strange presence.

This deserves to be unravelled in all its wider implications. It may be the biggest issue here, whatever the final verdict. How can this be the right thing? How can City’s fans look their own autocratic government-funded club in the eye? The quiet thing has been said out loud. And its implications are bigger than the game, bigger than legal opinion. Enough, perhaps to make you question the existential point of this thing, where the best course of action really might be to walk off and look for the nearest cheeseburger.

#849. EU moves to loosen rules on pesticide use as experts sound the alarm

The European Union wants to relax rules for pesticides, saying it will be easier for farmers to adopt more environmentally friendly options. But health and environmental experts say the risks are far too great.

As part of its drive to "streamline and simplify" EU laws, the European Commission has proposed sweeping changes for agriculture and food safety legislation. These include a move to ease rules controlling the use of pesticides and herbicides, which help fight pests and weeds.

Under current EU rules, which date back to 2011, primary pesticide components, or active substances, are only granted approval for limited periods of no more than 15 years.

The European Commission's proposed revamp of the system would make indefinite greenlighting — including of the controversial glyphosate, which has been linked to cancer and kills almost all plant life — the default. Safety reviews would only be done in exceptional cases, and regulatory authorities, not the industry, would bear responsibility.

The commission has said its goal is to cut costs, simplify work for authorities and help farmers stay competitive. Scientists and doctors, however, warn that concerns over human health and environmental impact from these toxic substances are being brushed aside.

The European Commission has said it's responding to complaints from farmers and the agriculture industry to clarify EU rules that govern pesticide use.

A joint statement released in May by 19 food associations, including CropLife Europe, which promotes pesticides, said complicated administrative procedures and a lengthy approvals process meant farmers were "left without any effective solutions to protect their crops against insects, weeds and diseases," putting food security and livelihoods at risk.

"The existing system of periodic renewal assessment of every active substance has become unsustainable," the commission's press service told DW, citing "chronic delays" and "bottlenecks" in the approval of new, more sustainable products.

In recent negotiations, EU member states said open-ended authorizations should be restricted to "low-risk active substances."

But their stance is still wanting to extend initial approval periods for other substances to up to 15 years, and a maximum of 25 years for renewals.

Herbert Dorfmann, a center-right Italian member of the European Parliament, said there is currently a yearslong delay in approving new pesticides, including more eco-friendly options, meaning farmers are forced to rely on older substances. Or, if these are banned, go without altogether.

The commission wants to "make the system more efficient and responsive," while guaranteeing that "the protection of human and animal health and the environment remain the highest priorities."

Dorfmann, who as co-rapporteur is responsible for interinstitutional negotiations on the issue, backs the commission's stance, saying the EU needs "to open up the system for innovation."

He aims to bring the parliament's proposal on the new pesticide rules to a vote among EU lawmakers before the end of the year.

Ecologists and medical experts, however, have spoken out forcefully against the proposed changes, saying the potential implications for human health and the environment are being downplayed.

In September, more than 500 experts from across the EU signed an open letter calling on the European Parliament to suspend its consideration of the new regulations and conduct an independent investigation into health and environmental impacts.

On October 7, UN rights experts also backed the call for a full review into whether the proposed changes violated the EU's obligations under international human rights law, especially with regard to agricultural workers and children.

Pesticides can persist in the environment, contaminating water and degrading soils. They can also drive biodiversity loss and poison other animals higher up the food chain.

When it comes to humans, the European Environment Agency has said it was "not yet possible to estimate the burden of disease linked to current levels of exposure to all pesticides."

However, exposure to chemical pesticides, including banned substances that still persist in the environment, has been linked to various cancers, chronic respiratory disease, neurological disorders and developmental delays, as well as problems with fertility and behavior.

And exposure is widespread: A survey conducted between 2014 and 2021 found that 84% of urine samples from both children and adults in five European countries contained residue from two or more pesticides.

Martina Vijver, scientific director and ecotoxicology expert at Leiden University in the Netherlands, said experts were "deeply concerned" that the EU's current plan "will weaken rather than strengthen the level of protection for pesticide regulation."

Speaking at the European Parliament in September, she said regular reassessments were key to evaluating the safety of pesticides with new findings, pointing out that the perception of risk changes over time.

"The regulatory system must remain capable of correcting yesterday's decisions with tomorrow's knowledge," she said.

Salome Roynel, a policy officer at the Pesticide Action Network Europe, an NGO based in Brussels, said the harmful effects of pesticides aren't often fully understood until years later, when the product is up for reconsideration.

"New science emerges all the time," she told DW, highlighting how 56 active substances have been banned in the EU since 2011 as a result of periodic reviews.

That includes the insecticide chlorpyrifos, previously used in orchards and on vegetable and cereal crops, which has been tied to harmful effects on children's brain development.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Roynel said it was "obvious that there was some kind of alignment" between the changes proposed by the EU institutions and the demands of the pesticide lobby.

This echoes a new report by nonprofit research and campaign group Corporate Europe Observatory, which said Dorfmann and other lawmakers had "copy-pasted […] industry demands" into their regulatory proposals.

Dorfmann denied the lobby influence, telling DW he had met with "both sides, industry and environmental associations," in public debates on the issue.

"The main objective is not to keep old products in the market. The main objective is to bring new ones to the market," Dorfmann said.

Part of that plan, he added, would be to help more environmentally friendly "biocontrol" products and low-risk substances to bypass current administrative hurdles and get on the market faster.

It's an idea previously championed by Vijver, who agrees that the current system means more environmentally friendly pesticides are stuck in an administrative "traffic jam." She told DW that biocontrol products could go in a green "bus lane" to ease the way to approval at the European Food Safety Authority, while maintaining crucial safety reviews to filter out the more dangerous products.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Roynel also supports the plan to speed up approval for biocontrol substances, but said it needs to be part of a wider system change that includes financial support, monitoring and training to use these new products, as well as maintaining the restrictions on more harmful chemical pesticides ― not further deregulation.

"If farmers get easier access to synthetic pesticides tomorrow, they would have no incentive to switch to biocontrol," she said. "It's important to put [biocontrol pesticides] on the market and we fully support that, but… it will not be the silver bullet."

#848. Grealish could have been Everton’s poster boy of a new era. Now his career is in limbo

After being dropped for ‘a breach of club discipline’, the winger must face the same questions about respect and self-awareness

For the biggest game in Manchester City’s history, Jack Grealish was given a starting berth while Phil Foden, Julián Alvarez and Riyad Mahrez were on the bench. Grealish played the full 90 minutes of the Champions League triumph against Inter because Pep Guardiola had the greatest faith in the attacking midfielder, but three years on he is at risk of being yesterday’s man.

That trust dwindled, not helped by injuries, and Grealish made only 17 Premier League starts over the next two seasons under Guardiola. City wanted him to leave in the summer of 2025, and Everton provided the solution, taking him on loan and borrowing him again for this season. Six Everton appearances into this campaign he was left out of the squad for Thursday’s Carabao Cup win against Newcastle after missing training on Monday. Everton went public with the fact that there had been “a breach of club discipline”.

Grealish is 31 and has 39 England caps. He is supposed to be a senior player but his career has involved far too many indiscretions. Breaking lockdown rules, a driving ban and more than once becoming a viral sensation for being pictured inebriated out and about have painted an unwanted picture. Learning from mistakes is part of life but Grealish’s indiscipline is apparently not dwindling with age. Guardiola warned him over his behaviour, dropping him in 2021 for a match against Newcastle after he and Foden arrived for training worse for wear.

Grealish is aware of his flaws, which is a starting point, but dealing with them is a separate matter. “People go: ‘He likes to go out, he likes to party,’ and I do,” Grealish told Sky Sports last year. “I want to be able to live my life and enjoy myself but obviously there’s a time and a place to do that. Sometimes, I’ll be honest with you, I probably haven’t picked the right times.”

Initially at Everton it seemed Grealish could be the poster boy of a new era. There were winners against Crystal Palace and Bournemouth by early December of last year and he had accumulated six assists in 20 Premier League appearances before his season was ended in mid-January by a foot injury. Grealish had been inconsistent, though. He has not played more than 28 league games in a season since 2019-20 at Aston Villa, which should concern him.

There were reservations at Everton about taking Grealish back this summer but Iliman Ndiaye’s sale to City made it a pragmatic move to fill the void. Grealish had carried out pre-season under Enzo Maresca, who gave him chances in the Community Shield and on the opening day against Bournemouth. The Italian had time for him but the unlikely redemption arc at City was soon quashed. Maresca showed affection for Grealish on Friday, saying: “I still think that he’s a good boy, big heart.”

At his best, Grealish is a wonderful player, a carefree spirit when dribbling with his socks around his ankles. In full flow, he gets fans up off their seats, makes and takes goalscoring chances and forces opponents to foul him, but those moments have been fleeting for far too long. The next seven months are crucial to Grealish’s career; he is at an age where he could play at the top for years but his status is declining rapidly. He is a £100m City signing and treble winner but those are past glories. Grealish needs to prove he has the respect for himself and for Everton to want more.

Grealish’s contract at City concludes at the end of the season, so there is plenty of incentive for him to show he is capable of shining in the Premier League and inspiring Everton to the cup win they crave. Instead, his career is in limbo. David Moyes was terse on the subject of Grealish on Thursday and seems unlikely to recommend keeping him beyond his loan. The Everton manager is working with a very small squad, so losing a senior player for avoidable reasons will surely frustrate and irritate him.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

In an industry where the public is kept at arm’s length, Grealish is very approachable, happy to sign autographs for longer than his peers, eager to do the charity elements that come with playing for major clubs and known for his personal touch when others are businesslike. When entering and leaving Hill Dickinson Stadium, Grealish is mobbed, such is his popularity. He embraces it, posing for selfies with anyone who demands one, channelling a lot of positive energy into others, but he needs to find the self-awareness to do the same for himself.

“With me, I’m a big confidence player – I want to feel loved,” Grealish once said. He will not be feeling that from Moyes any time soon without radical change.

#847. Manchester United’s capitulation at Chelsea paints picture of a club that barely exists | Barney Ronay

Michael Carrick is now a little more pre-doomed, pre-sacked, but is miles away from being the actual story

On and on and on. And then on just a little bit more it would seem. Manchester United: always crashing in the same Carrick.

The obvious question after this 2-0 defeat against Chelsea is how much longer United will continue to lose games under the current manager, as opposed to losing games under the next one. But it is also a mark of the dysfunction of this club, its ambient levels of sadness, that this matters so little.

Here we have another staging point in the progress of the Manchester United ghost ship, where even sacking a manager carries almost zero tension, where it feels like something that has basically already happened. This is a club that can make you into a relic of the past even while you’re still walking around taking training and drawing a salary.

Michael Carrick is miles away from being the actual story here. For the record, the United manager is now a little more pre-doomed, pre-sacked, pretty much already lounging around in one of those food delivery adverts with Tony Pulis joshing about what’s for lunch. This defeat means United haven’t won a game since early September. At full time only the fact that Coventry and Sunderland would be playing each other later in the afternoon ruled out the prospect of an end‑of‑day bottom place.

Chuck in a Carabao Cup exit and 2oth spot in the Champions League mega-table. Troubled times, then, for the latest semi-permanent navy wool suit in the United dugout. Something will now happen, most likely Carrick’s removal once the appropriate replacement is lined up. What happened here was almost by the by. Although it still provided some pretty vivid evidence of where this club is.

If there was a key moment, it arrived with 50 minutes gone and the score still 0-0. At which point Morgan Rogers scored a goal that captured entirely what Manchester United is. In real time, this felt like one of those football moments, where the metaphor, the symbolism is almost too much, the nudge in the ribs a little too hard.

Rogers took the ball on the edge of the centre circle and just kept running in a straight line through sudden empty spaces where there should have been a thing called Manchester United. Instead he found an anti-United, a non‑United. Manchester United as an absence. So much analysis of this club evolves around what is it for, where should it turn, what can it be? Maybe it’s not really anything at all.

We do remember Manchester United. It has a cultural memory, a set of shapes and colours, a gripping centre. Or does it? There was once a dream that was Manchester United. You could whisper its name. Anything more than a whisper and it would vanish. So Rogers just kept running in a straight line, moving fast now, finding no resistance, nothing of substance, fibre, no flesh, no will in front of him, like opening up the curtains and watching the shadows disappear.

How many times has this happened at this level, that a player is able to take the ball and run 40 yards through a packed opposition half without having to dribble, beat a player or even swerve around some tangible object?

This is not to diminish Rogers’ skill and drive. The finish was really nice, a little dink as Senne Lammens came out and made a strange shape, as confused as anyone else by the sudden appearance of a living, moving, actual human in front of him.

Teams are often described as having been found out, their patterns solved and learned. It turns out this is the way to score against Manchester United. Just run straight through the middle of them.

Before long it was time for Lisandro Martínez to get sent off, again playing football that wasn’t really there. Chelsea took a corner from the right. At which point Martínez rammed his arm into Wesley Fofana’s neck with the ball miles away. Maybe Martínez just wanted to touch another human being. Sometimes you just need to feel something.

Cole Palmer buried the penalty to make the score 2-0, with United a man down and not existing, just a little bit more.

And OK, OK, you’re still thinking about the good news, aren’t you? Well, presumably Sir Jim Ratcliffe will see the material gain here, the chance to save on hotel costs with another nonexistent team. No, we don’t need any rooms. We are non-corporeal.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

On a more positive note, at least the players are annoyed. Really. It has been seen as a sign of dysfunction, the ravens leaving the Tower, that United’s senior players have begun to speak in public. But wouldn’t it be weird if they didn’t? What is the correct human response to this state of complete, top-down lack of care, of managed disintegration?

The first half was lively enough. Bruno Fernandes was back in the United starting XI on a lovely crisp October morning, the sun sharp but soft, the grass a deep lime green. It is said that United lack leaders. But what is a leader? Someone who shows you how to win, makes winning more likely, walks you right to the door. Well, good luck with that around here. The Sahara desert also lacks grass. This isn’t really the fault of grass.

And so Manchester United started with one bloke who thinks the hierarchy has betrayed the club and another who thinks the manager is tactically poor. The thing is, they’re both right. Fernandes in particular broke the code, undermining his manager, talking tactics when you are housefly playing like a performatively unhappy jack russell.

But it is hard to blame the players too much for losing the run of themselves a little. This is a club that takes a bite out of everyone, that makes everything wrong, a club that spends and spends and still seems short, that is somehow ludicrously profitable, but also ludicrously in debt, where to be a supporter is to be left always feeling short-changed, owed so much more.

By the end the game had basically become a shooting practice session for Chelsea, who were good, even if they were playing a team that didn’t exist. The most significant element was the performance of Estêvão Willian, who tortured Diogo Dalot on the right flank. When Estêvão came off the home crowd stood on all sides. He is very obviously going to be a proper player.

The last knockings were accompanied by the familiar shots on the big screen of Omar Berrada and Jason Wilcox looking doomed and sombre, in a way that was arguably the most sustained United performance of the afternoon. You try looking sombre for the cameras for 90 minutes. It is at the very least a sign of some excellent media training (no, Jason, you look wistful, I need urgently alarmed).

These people will now pronounce on Michael Carrick, who they hired knowing he was Michael Carrick. But who shall pronounce on them? And will it make any difference, unless someone pronounces on the people who pronounce on the people who pronounce on every single area of interim mediocrity installed at this giant ATM of a football club. Root out the problem. Well, we can do that. But we’re going to need new roots, bark, branches, leaves.

When it comes to Carrick, everybody knows United are just waiting, finger hovering over the gunge tank. Alternatives are being lined up, terms thrashed out. There is an international break soon. Funny, isn’t it? An organisation of squawking, howling incompetence. But the one place you feel suddenly in the hands of the experts, safe hands, is this part. Stand back, let the experts in. Masters of the mid‑season sacking. Seen it, done it. We know this world.

Carrick has played his part well through all this and said all the right things. He is what he is: a coach who is not at the peak of his profession, who is engaged in weekly micro-battles with people who are. It’s not his fault he’s not cut out for this level. He didn’t hire Michael Carrick.

As for the rest of this thing, the ghost players, the latest pressed men and padded overcoats in the seats of power; they continue to perform to their own level too, at an organisation that has by now fully embraced mediocrity and misdirection as a business plan.

#846. Turkey's new deal on Mediterranean maritime boundaries with Libya is exacerbating issues with Greece and the EU

Turkey and Libya plan to redraw maritime boundaries in the Mediterranean as part of a new economic corridor. This has sparked strong protests from Greece, and has also drawn the European Union into the conflict.

On Tuesday, the parliament of Libya unanimously approved a maritime agreement with Turkey to establish a direct maritime economic corridor between the countries.

Turkey had agreed on the corridor with the UN-recognized Government of National Accord in western Libya in 2019. However, the agreement faced opposition from the rival Libyan government in the country's east. Now, though, the eastern parliament has reversed its previous opposition.

The decision, which was welcomed by Turkey's Foreign Ministry, is likely to contribute to tensions with other countries in the eastern Mediterranean — especially Greece .

The agreement establishes a direct maritime corridor between the southern coast of Turkey and the northern coast of Libya. Large oil and gas deposits have recently been discovered in the region in question — estimates suggest that natural gas reserves worth several hundred billion US dollars may lie beneath the seabed. Turkey and Libya aim to secure their economic rights to these raw materials and are seeking to jointly exploit the resources.

The planned corridor disregards Greek islands such as Crete, Karpathos and Rhodes. Greece's government insists that it possesses a comprehensive exclusive economic zone, or EEZ, around these islands and has already announced its opposition to the accord.

In a post on X, the Foreign Ministry announced that Greece firmly rejects the agreement and has the support of the European Union in doing so. "The European Union has described the Turkish-Libyan memorandum as null and void, stressing that it violates the sovereign rights of third states and is not consistent with the Law of the Sea," the ministry posted.

Similar wording came straight from Brussels. "I raised yesterday's Libyan vote on a maritime MoU with Türkiye and stressed that it infringes upon the sovereign rights of third states," Kaja Kallas, the European Union high representative for foreign affairs and security policy, posted on X.

Whose claims are legitimate in the eastern Mediterranean is the central point of contention. Greece primarily cites the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, or UNCLOS. According to Article 121 of the convention, inhabited islands that "support an economic life of their own” have the same rights to an EEZ as the mainland. This applies to Crete, Rhodes and Lesbos.

Athens cites precedents such as a 2022 ruling by the International Court of Justicethat found that Colombia had violated the sovereign rights of Nicaragua by authorizing fishing activities in the Central American country's EEZ. The ICJ found that when interests overlap a fair demarcation must be reached that takes coastlines, geographical conditions and the implications of a potential boundary into account.

Turkey's government argues that the geography of the Mediterranean plays a special role: If every small Greek island off the coast of Turkey and Cyprus  were granted a full EEZ, Turkey would be largely cut off from access to the open sea. This, the government argues, must be given greater consideration when demarcating the boundary.

Unlike Greece, Turkey has never signed UNCLOS. Therefore, it does not agree to have the dispute heard by a UN arbitration tribunal. Moreover, even international experts on the law of the sea disagree on what a "fair division” might look like in this specific case.

When Turkey pushed for the agreement in 2019, a brutal civil war was still raging in Libya. At that time, Turkey intervened militarily in the west to support the government in Tripoli, thereby repelling the offensive by eastern Libyan General Khalifa Hifter.

Since then, the relationship has changed fundamentally: A successful charm offensive by Turkey's government appears to have led to a political rapprochement with Hifter and his camp. Turkey's government now maintains mutually advantageous relations with both parts of Libya. In addition to the countries' plan to develop energy resources in the Mediterranean together, Turkish construction companies have secured contracts worth billions in recent years for Libya's reconstruction. Furthermore, the Turkish state-owned oil company TPAO and the Libyan National Oil Corporation are already working on joint plans for seismic surveys off of Libya's coast.

Turkey's government has established itself as a new military partner for Hifter's forces, supplying weapons and offering training programs. In doing so, Turkey is pushing back against the influence of Egypt and Russia in eastern Libya and strengthening its role as a geopolitical player in the region.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

With the agreement now approved in the regional parliament, eastern Libya also aims to secure its share of the lucrative natural resources. This could give Hifter greater international influence in the future. Disputes in the eastern Mediterranean are likely to escalate further as a result of the agreement — particularly once Turkey and Libya begin extracting oil and gas from the disputed maritime area.

The agreement also jeopardizes a major project that is still in the planning stages: the EastMed pipeline, which is intended to transport natural gas from Israel and Cyprus via Greece, thereby making an important contribution to energy security in the European Union. However, the corridor established by Turkey and Libya cuts across the planned route of the pipeline. Turkey has also argued that projects involving cables or pipelines on its claimed continental shelf require its consent.

In the long term, this could lead to a division of the eastern Mediterranean region into two competing energy and defense blocs: The Turkey-Libya axis might be countered by an EU-supported alliance of Greece, Cyprus, Egypt and Israel.

It took her six hours to get ready on Oct. 31, but her team has been working for months to create the prosthetics—or, as she quipped, "Many hands doing this hand."

#841. Somewhere over the transcontinental burrito tunnel

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Elitsa Dermendzhiyska is a BSFA-nominated writer, a former science writer in psychology, and the co-creator of a mental-health fantasy game. Her stories have appeared in Flash Fiction Online, Small Wonders, Flame Tree Press and others.

Lenny fell in love with Bea around burrito number five. He recognized that dizzying jolt to his brain the instant the tunnel’s mouth sighed with a sweet pneumatic hiss and the vacuum-sealed burrito glided in.

Three hours and twenty-one minutes earlier, 2,553 miles away, at her end of the tunnel in the East Bay facility, Bea had been thinking of him. She must have. He wished he could trace her regard for his existence beyond the minute or two it would’ve taken her to pluck the flash-chilled burrito from the sorting dock, nest it in its carbon-fibre pod, and send it in the near-vacuum of the tunnel deep into the Earth to be blasted across the continent at just below the speed of sound.

Lenny worked the subterranean off-ramp in New Jersey, where multitudes of the famed Mission burritos of the Bay Area arrived levitating on magnetic currents, ready for dispatch to the ravenous gullets of the five boroughs of New York City. Since the blast aboveground, the flow had dwindled to one burrito at a time. Lenny stared at each with longing, wondering if Bea had tucked a note for him into the Mylar pocket.

When her first message arrived, the eerie rumble still vibrated through the basement walls. Lenny was pacing in circles, running through scenarios — alien invasion, given the contact the year before; nuclear war, given … many things — and going mad at the thought of dying underground, alone. He was ready to venture out and face the radiation or the new overlords when the first burrito slid out with a note attached to it. Here: an end-of-the-world burrito. Best you’ve ever had.

Read more science fiction from Nature Futures

Read more science fiction from Nature Futures

Apparently Bea had never expected her message to reach anyone. Who knew insomnia would drive them both to work before clock-in time, saving them? Now she was sitting on a dragon’s hoard of burritos, that morning’s shipment enough to feed them both for weeks. They could stay put, wait for things to blow over.

The problem wasn’t food — or the aliens, or the bombs. It was, as usual with Lenny, love.

Around burrito number nine, he wrote on a whim, Folks might get the wrong impression if they saw you spoiling me. He slipped his note into a Mylar pouch, which he placed inside an empty burrito pod and sent down the tube.

Bea volleyed back, Yeah, they’ll think you’re my grandson. PS What folks, Lenny???

He chewed through the cold tortilla. Was she flirting back? Or letting him down gently by hinting at her age? Which wouldn’t be an issue.

Lenny agonized over his retort for hours, maybe even days. Afterwards, every exchange between him and Bea felt loaded with subtext. Chorizo with Mexican red rice, refried pinto beans and real Monterey Jack, Bea wrote. Enjoy :) Was a smiley face coy or merely friendly? What about one with a wink?

Lenny talked to her in his head, Bea nodding, her dark eyes dancing. But whenever he put pen to paper, his lucidity evaporated, crumbling to the overeager babble of a hapless nitwit.

At one point, Bea wrote, A day is a long time.

He stared at the plastic sleeve, yearning to sweep her into his arms. He placed his hands where her own had been three hours and twenty-one minutes earlier.

Are you bored, too? Lenny replied. I thought we could pass the time by getting to know each other. He proceeded to tell her about his favourite music and where he’d grown up, including several major formative events from his childhood.

After what felt like eternity, Bea wrote back. It was an ingredient list. Carne asada, sautéed mushrooms and salsa verde.

What’s happening, Bea? What’d I do? he wrote.

Several torturous hours passed. Then: Imagine a map of an island, alright? It’s the most high-fidelity, super-detailed map of the place there is. Now imagine the map itself is on the island. You see what that means? There must be a map of the map inside the map. And inside that second map — another one. On and on. It’s maps all the way down, Lenny.

Lenny had heard a paradox like this somewhere before. But Bea seemed to be opening up at last. Her scrawls looked frantic, streaking across the margins like startled flamingos. He turned the riddle around and around, then wrote back, What about the map maker? Is he also in all of the maps drawing them … and himself?

#840. Rampant Salford hint that Beckham’s lofty ambitions are not a pipe dream

The aim of reaching the Championship looks more realistic for a Manchester club in the shadow of City and United

After seven seasons in League Two, Salford City are finally threatening to match the hype brought by their high-profile owners. First it was the Class of ’92 who guided them up through the non-league system into the fourth tier but failed to progress any further. Gary Neville and David Beckham remain, part of a new group that took over in May 2025, with this year beginning to look transformational after securing an eighth straight win, against Exeter, to put them five points clear at the top.

The budget has increased, allowing the club to sign a number of players who will feel they are above League Two standard. Striker Macaulay Langstaff arrived from Millwall; the last time he played at this level, he scored 28 league goals in a season for Notts County. Match-winner Will Aimson spent the past two seasons in the division above with Wigan and has dropped down because of Salford’s project.

In terms of personnel, the most notable change was in the dugout where 48-year-old Peter Cklamovski replaced Karl Robinson, who was sacked after a desperate performance in the playoff final loss to Notts County. Cklamovski’s previous experience came working under Ange Postecoglou before becoming a head coach in his own right in Asia, most recently taking charge of the Malaysia national team. Such was his unknown status, Salford’s chief football adviser Paul Scholes had to Google the Australian before he was appointed.

Off the pitch, Salford reverted to wearing orange, the traditional club colour that was changed by the Class of ’92, who wanted the shirts to reflect their links to Manchester United. The fans voted for it, democracy in action where previously the owners knew best. Beckham has turned Inter Miami into a global brand worth more than £1bn, making pink a key part of its identity. Lionel Messi shirt sales helped the hue travel, with kids across the UK spotted with the famous No 10 on the back. Beckham selected the shade of orange – and the badge was redesigned – but whether Langstaff et al can have the same effect as Messi remains to be seen. “Not many others play in orange, so if you’re going to see that kit around Manchester, you would know it’s not United or City,” says Danny Shepherd of The Future Is Orange podcast.

Attracting new fans is the aim but Salford face competition from much bigger clubs in the region. Even with Manchester City in a crisis and United’s form spiralling, convincing locals to head down to the AIG Stadium is difficult. Cklamovski’s attractive style is a deliberate ploy but the Ammies have the fourth-worst average attendance in League Two. It is optimistic to think they can create a Championship fanbase, even with subsidised away travel.

Cklamovski is making a name for himself with the aggressive attacking football he learned under his mentor. He started with three defeats but since then the Australian has found a pragmatic approach, mixing his playing out from the back ideals with an openness to be more direct when required, which brought a change in fortunes.

“I’d be disappointed if we didn’t go up because of the strength in depth,” says Shepherd. “Last season we had certain linchpin players that if they weren’t available, then we had either a utility player, a youngster or someone whose quality is so much lower that it’s like falling off a cliff. I’m not a rose-tinted spectacles fan, I can’t see how this team cannot get promoted – I think we should win the league at a canter.”

The confidence was not fully apparent in the first half as Salford were sloppy and struggled to create chances, while defensively vulnerable against a resolute Exeter. Goalkeeper Will Norris was booked for rushing out of his area and fouling Sonny Cox, who got his own back by scoring the opener for a side on a fine run themselves, unbeaten in the previous five.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Salford only came to life after the disappointing Luke Molyneux was forced off through injury, replaced by Daniel Udoh in the 55th minute. Energy levels increased and were rewarded by Luke Garbutt’s leveller at the back post after Langstaff’s fine work on the right.

Salford were on top after that and got their reward from the unfamiliar source of former Exeter centre-back Aimson, who sent a shot into the top corner from 25 yards to keep the run going and show this team have character to battle back in difficult circumstances. “We’ve got to stay really focused and diligent,” Cklamovski says. “We’ve got a nice bit of momentum, but don’t look too far forward. Eight wins in a row or 11 unbeaten however you want to look at it, just don’t look back.” He need not worry, there are plenty of people above him looking to the future.

#838. Heidi Klum's Kids Lou, Johan and Leni Have Rare Outing for Halloween

Heidi Klum’s kids Leni Klum, 22, Johan Samuel, 19, and Lou Samuel, 17, followed in her footsteps with their Halloween spirit, making a rare joint appearance at her party Oct. 31.

Heidi Klum's kids didn't need a hand with their Halloween costumes this year.

The supermodel's children Leni Klum, 22, Johan Samuel, 19, and Lou Samuel, 17, proved they've got more than skeletons in their closet as they were dressed in their Halloween finest while making a rare joint appearance at her annual party at Cathédrale Restaurant in New York Oct. 31.

For their mom’s annual spooky season bash, Leni—whom Heidi shares with ex Flavio Briatore—transformed into a diva as Miss Piggy, with a white nightgown, a purple feather boa, pig ears and a prosthetic nose.

Lou channeled Starfire from Teen Titans, rocking a purple costume as the superheroine on the red carpet alongside brother Johan, who looked frighteningly good with zombie makeup.

As for the Queen of Halloween herself, while Heidi dressed in a terrifying Medusa costume at her 2025 event—her husband Tom Kaulitz appearing as one of her stone victims—this year the model leaned even further to the grotesque, pulling together a chilling costume that was truly larger than life.

Yep, the 53-year-old—also mom to Henry, 21, with ex-husband Seal—once again proved she isn’t afraid to look terrifyingly disgusting, arriving to her party as a severed hand.

"It was about six hours to get ready, but obviously my team they spent months on doing this," Heidi told E!. "Many people, many hands doing this hand."

It even included a nod to husband, as her costume replicated her real wedding ring and her tattoo on the back of her ring finger bearing Tom's name.

While her exact costume remained under wraps until Halloween, she did tease her 2026 costume a week before the bash.

“What’s my costume?” Heidi wrote alongside a zoomed in shot of her costume on Oct. 24. “One week to go….”

The close up revealed what looked to be prosthetic pieces in various colors and textures—including slime. While the photo didn’t reveal exactly what Heidi’s costume would be, fans speculated the look might be aquatic in nature in the comment section, while others wondered if she was aspiring to imitate the zombies in The Last of Us or the creature from the 2024 film The Substance.

And while the reality proved to hit even more close to home that fans could have imagined, they shouldn’t have been surprised by the gore.

Heidi told People back in September this year’s costume would be “very, very bloody.”

“That’s what Halloween is all about,” she emphasized. “We go gory, and we go there.”

And go there she did. To see how other celebrities brewed up a terrifyingly good costume for Heidi’s party, read on.

The model's costume is hands down one of her best, as she dressed as her real left hand—including her wedding ring from husband Tom Kaulitz.

The couple was unrecognizable as the twins from The Shining at Heidi Klum’s 25th annual Halloween Party.

Attending alongside his wife, the Sex and the City star was dressed as "the evil" Cliff Vandercave from his 1994 movie The Flintstones.

"This is a blast from the past with Flintstones," he told E!. "Original costume. I don't think they know it's gone, so don't tell them."

Klum's kids banded together on the red carpet for the party, which was presented by Apothic and Butterfinger at Cathédrale in New York City.

#837. In Bulgaria, record low voter turnout triggers a November 1 presidential run-off in a poll colored by divisions over Ukraine war

Low voter turnout has triggered a run-off for the Bulgarian presidency. The vote was colored by strong divisions over Russia's war in Ukraine, and Sofia's relations with the Kremlin.

Record low turnout in Sunday's Bulgarian elections mean voters are expected to head to the polls on November 1 to cast ballots in a presidential run-off.

Polling stations opened at 7 a.m. and closed at 8 p.m. (0500-1800 GMT), with official results expected within 48 hours, but voter turnout was less than 40%, far short of the 50% required.

Voters were choosing between candidates with vastly different views of the war in Ukraine and relations with Moscow and the vote came as drone attacks on ships in the Black Sea off the Bulgarian coast brought home the significance of the conflict in Ukraine for the former Soviet satellite state.

Although the presidency is largely ceremonial, the head of state in Bulgaria can appoint interim governments during political crises, is commander-in-chief of the armed forces and is able to veto legislation.

Frontrunner in the elections is incumbent President Iliana Yotova, who took over the position this year after current Prime Minister Rumen Radev stepped down to take part in the parliamentary elections that led him to power.

Yotova, 62, who surveys show as having 41-47% of the vote, favors dialogue with Moscow as the way to bring peace to Ukraine and opposes military aid to Kyiv.

A win for Yotova would give a boost for Radev, who also advocates dialogue with Moscow. Victory would make Yotova Bulgaria’s first elected female president.

Her main challenger is Andrey Gyurov, a former caretaker prime minister, who is polling at 28-31%.

Gyurov, 50, who is backed by the pro-Western opposition, is an outspoken critic of Radev's foreign policy and strongly supports the Euro-Atlantic ties of Bulgaria, a European Union and NATO member state. As caretaker prime minister, Gyurov signed a security cooperation agreement with Kyiv.

The leader of the pro-Russian far-right Vazrazhdane party, Kostadin Kostadinov, is in third place on 10-13%.

Altogether 27 pairs of candidates for president and vice president are competing in the first round, with nearly half of them openly pro-Kremlin.

After casting her ballot in Sofia, Yotova called for peace, stability and unity, urging an end to divisions among Bulgarians. Her main challenger, Gyurov, voted in Blagoevgrad, calling for a Bulgaria that looks ahead and offers families greater economic security. Turnout was estimated at 15.1% by 3 p.m. local time (1300 GMT), according to polling agency Myara, Bulgarian media reported.

To win outright, a candidate must secure more than half the valid votes, with more than half of eligible voters taking part. Otherwise, the top two candidates advance to a runoff on November 1.

The war in Ukraine triggered by Russia's unprovoked invasion is one of the central themes in the election, particularly after four merchant ships were allegedly hit by drones off Bulgaria's coast this month in suspected spillover from the conflict. The attacks have prompted Bulgaria to seek assistance from its allies to strengthen maritime security.

Satellite internet antennas from the Starlink network — an important part of Ukraine's defense capabilities — were also set on fire near the capital, Sofia.

While Radev has said that the attacks seemed to be to the advantage of Russia and summoned the Russian ambassador, his government has declined to blame the incidents directly on Moscow.

The strikes have nonetheless raised concerns over Russia’s intentions to escalate the conflict.

Rising energy prices and inflation that have caused economic hardship to many in Bulgaria, the EU's poorest member state, are also a main issue addressed by candidates.

Many voters are also looking to stop government corruption, a persistent concern in the country, and hope for a stable government after multiple elections and coalition breakdowns in recent years.

#832. Kyle MacLachlan Reveals If He'd Ever Return to SATC Franchise

Kyle MacLachlan exclusively told E! News if he’d be interested in reprising his role as Sex and the City’s Trey MacDougal again, given the chance, while at Heidi Klum's Halloween party in NYC.

Kyle MacLachlan couldn’t help but wonder...what Trey MacDougal is doing today.

After the Sex and the City alum did not reprise his character as Charlotte York’s ex-husband in the sequel series And Just Like That, he shared whether or not he’d say alrighty to stepping into Trey’s shoes if a potential future installment were to happen once more.

“Oh, would I ever! Absolutely,” MacLachlan exclusively told E! News at Heidi Klum's 25th Annual Halloween Party at Cathédrale in New York City Oct. 31. “Come on, Trey has to come back.”

"He's got unfinished business,” he continued. “Of course, that would be fun.”

MacLachlan—who was joined by his son Callum, 18, at the star-studded spooky soiree—playfully noted that he was ready to “start some vicious rumors” of Trey’s return in a new spinoff series.

“It’s going to happen, very, very soon,” he joked at the event, which was presented by Apothic and Butterfinger. “I know this is going to get picked up and going to be the logline and that’s how it’s going to work.”

And while it’s been nearly 25 years since the 67-year-old last appeared as Trey—the first husband of Kristin Davis’ Charlotte—in season four in 2002, he still remembers the time fondly.

“There are very many memories,” MacLachlan, who dressed as an “evil” Cliff Vandercave from The Flintstones at Klum’s Halloween party, shared. “I think working with Kristin Davis is one of my most favorite. We had a really wonderful run. I love her dearly, and she's so wonderful. And so anytime working with her was special.”

In fact, the Twin Peaks alum still keeps up with Davis, as well as other former members of the SATC cast and crew.

“I still see her occasionally,” MacLachlan said of Davis. “Occasionally I see Chris [Noth] out and about. [Showrunner] Michael Patrick King and then we're good friends with Darren Starr, who was the original creator of it. So, we stay in touch with a few of them.”

#830. Hemp strikes back as Manchester City edge out London City Lionesses in thriller

Goals from Khadija Shaw and Lauren Hemp helped Manchester City to escape from Bromley with three points after a thrilling encounter with London City Lionesses. It was a statement performance from the home team, despite the defeat delivering a blow to any title ambitions they may have been quietly holding on to before kick-off.

The gap between the hosts and the champions is now six points, after Hemp restored City’s lead following Jana Fernández’s equaliser. But that London City had even played their way into conversations about this season’s title contenders in their second season has been impressive.

Andrée Jeglertz, the Manchester City manager, praised the ability of his team to win in different ways as needed, after three games in eight days. “We said afterwards, the players should be so proud of what they put into this game,” he said.

“We’ve learned we’re a great team who can keep the ball for 75% of the game and win that way, or we can win like this. That quality to win in different ways is good to have, but the players also have to adapt to that and feel it’s OK to not have the ball all the time, take pride in defending and only having three or four chances but finishing off those chances.”

Before kick-off, cameras showed London City’s superstar summer signing Alexia Putellas opening the boot of her car and taking out a heavy leather-clad square item, her third Ballon d’Or safely encased inside. The Spain midfielder did not present her trophy to fans in the stands before kick-off, instead choosing to put it on display so supporters could queue to have their photo taken with it.

The only nod to the player’s stunning individual year, in which she won the quadruple with Barcelona before joining London City, was on her feet, the geometric gold on her custom Ballon d’Or-themed boots glinting on their first outing.

There have been jokes aplenty about the unlikelihood of the world’s premier individual award heading to its new Bromley home. To reach the stadium from Hayes Lane, you pass a field of horses on your left. London City Lionesses are not Barcelona, and they have become the home of the Ballon d’Or winner by default rather than being the key component of that individual success.

Except, based on the season London City are having and the ruthless ambitions of the owner, Michelle Kang, the idea that the club could produce a season that delivers them collective success and individual success off the back of it feels less distant than it did just a few short months ago.

Against the champions, London City more than held their own, the opportunity to move level on points with their opponents and league leaders Chelsea an inviting incentive. Their threat was evident within 30 seconds, when the Manchester City defender Rebecca Knaak was forced to turn Lucía Corrales’s cross wide of the far post just ahead of a waiting Isobel Goodwin.

Neither team has impressed defensively this season, each only managing to keep one clean sheet in the Women’s Super League, and it made for a thrilling encounter, the high lines and aggressiveness of both attacks delivering a showstopper.

Making her first WSL start for the home team, with Elene Lete hitherto preferred, Mary Earps made a huge statement with an impressive double save from a Knaak header to keep the game goalless going into the break.

No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football

City broke the deadlock despite London City dominating and it was their most influential player who delivered. Hemp flicked the ball into the run of Shaw and with her first touch, she took it past Earps before she switched the ball on to her right foot and fired in to become just the third player to score in eight consecutive WSL starts.

A deserved equaliser arrived in the 72nd minute, when Fernández was at the near post to meet a corner and her assured header sent the ball looping in at the back post.

The celebrations were emphatic but they were short-lived. This is a new, more resilient Manchester City, one that survived various scares last term to secure a second WSL title, and they re-established their lead two minutes later, when Hemp stretched out a leg to poke in Mary Fowler’s cross from the right to secure the win.

That London City could feel aggrieved at having not taken something from the game was a testament to their performance and how quickly progress is being made. The home team had 23 shots to City’s seven and 52 touches in the opposition box to City’s 13, but critically the visiting team were clinical when it mattered. Converting two of their three efforts on target and showing the edge needed to battle at the top.

#828. European football: Mbappé penalty helps Real Madrid stroll to sixth straight win

Bellingham and Diomandé complete 3-0 win over Racing

Lazio top Serie A after fighting back to beat Cagliari

Kylian Mbappé moved on from a tumultuous week by scoring a penalty to help Real Madrid win 3-0 at Racing Santander on Sunday.

The French forward narrowly lost out on the Ballon d’Or to Bayern Munich’s Harry Kane on Monday and then had to apologise after a social media storm following a video in which he joked about the former Chinese leader Mao Zedong.

Real Madrid’s match, along with other Spanish fixtures this weekend, was not broadcast by Chinese state television because of the fallout.

Jude Bellingham and Yan Diomandé were also on target to keep third-placed Madrid within three points of the La Liga leaders, Barcelona, who thrashed Alavés 6-1 on Saturday.

José Mourinho’s side have won six straight games across all competitions and are a point behind Atlético Madrid, who beat Levante 2-0.

Real Sociedad’s four-match winning run came to an end after they lost 2-1 to Athletic Bilbao thanks to first-half goals from Inaki Williams and Alex Berenguer, who scored a penalty.

Gennaro Gattuso’s Lazio consolidated their position at the top of Serie A with a 2-1 victory over Cagliari, nudging ahead of Inter after the two clubs had started the weekend level on points.

Lazio made a poor start as Cagliari took the lead through M’Bala Nzola in the 20th minute before goals in either half from Gustav Isaksen and Andrea Pinamonti gave them a sixth straight Serie A win.

Como moved back into the top four as they eked out a 1-0 victory at home over bottom side Venezia on Sunday for a fifth consecutive victory across all competitions.

The hosts dominated, but needed a penalty to find the back of the net. The Como captain, Lucas Da Cunha, converted in the 43rd minute for the French international’s first goal of the season. “This is the type of match we found hard to win last season,” Da Cunha told Dazn.

Second-half goals from Kerim Alajbegovic and Jérémie Boga ensured Juventus returned to winning ways with a 2-0 victory over 10-man Napoli, who had Luca Marianucci sent off in the second half as they slipped to their fourth defeat of the campaign.

Lyon and Paris FC both won to close in on the defending Ligue 1 champions, Paris Saint-Germain, with the capital team defeating Monaco 3-1.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Lyon won 2-0 at home to Angers with goals in each half from Ernest Nuamah and Corentin Tolisso, as they bounced back from a 2-0 defeat away to PSG last time out.

The seven-time French title winners are third in the table, three points behind PSG and one behind second-placed Lille. Lyon’s win came amid reports that their coach, Paulo Fonseca, is close to leaving the club to return to his native Portugal.

“I know that I will be with the players tomorrow morning but beyond that it is hard to say,” Fonseca, who was in tears as he embraced his backroom staff at the end of the game, said. Fonseca is reportedly a target for Sporting, whose coach Rui Borges is under pressure.

Paris FC are fourth after getting the better of Monaco at the Stade Jean-Bouin. Lassine Sinayoko, the Malian international forward, scored twice late in the first half for Paris FC before Folarin Balogun pulled one back on 65 minutes.

#827. Kilmarnock 'need support more than ever' but patience wearing thin

Kilmarnock let a lead slip twice against 10-man St Johnstone on Saturday

Four goals shared, some excellent football played, and a plethora of chances created by the home side. All greeted on the final whistle by a loud, piercing chorus of boos and some angry finger-pointing by sections of the Kilmarnock support.

That such fan fury follows a result that actually moved the Ayrshire side off the bottom of the Scottish Premiership tells its own story.

The patience of the Rugby Park regulars appears to be wearing thin. A worry for under-pressure manager Neil McCann, whose side have only enjoyed two league wins all season.

To fail to beat St Johnstone at home when the visitors played for 80 minutes with 10 men would be a difficult one for any manager to swallow, never mind one for whom every win must feel like a life jacket in stormy sea.

"The most galling thing is they've scored two goals with 10 men - that's a sore one," McCann told BBC Scotland.

"We need the support more than ever. The players are working with everything they've got. There's no lack of willingness or effort to win games.

"We're all hurting that we don't win the games. We haven't lost the game today, but it feels like a loss because we dropped two points from a good position.

"Do I feel the pressure? No. I feel it for the boys because they're getting pressure applied."

It's not that Kilmarnock played badly. They didn't.

That match statistics back that up. McCann's men carved out 22 goal attempts - their highest total in a league match all season. They also attempted 542 passes - their highest in a single Premiership game this term.

It shouldn't be forgotten, of course, that they played against 10 men for most of the match. That's the hardest pill for the manager to swallow.

"The amount of chances we created... we just didn't take them, " McCann said. "That being said, a man up, 2-1 up, you shouldn't lose two points.

"Sometimes when you're a man up it's difficult because that team are working ever so hard - it's difficult to play against and it requires patience."

That could be the biggest problem the former Rangers and Hearts winger faces. Patience in modern football is usually in extremely short supply.

Having lost their previous two matches, a return of one point from the past available nine won't soothe any grumbles with an already disaffected support.

"I felt the uneasiness around the stadium, even when we were 2-1 up," he added. "And the players looked like they were being affected by it."

"We rushed things and, when it gets to 2-2, with lots of time left, there's no need to panic. We got into good areas, but we just lacked that quality."

The problem for McCann, and Kilmarnock, is that their last match before the international break is away to the defending champions and league leaders, Celtic.

Martin O'Neill's men scored five at Rugby Park in August. On their past three trips to Glasgow's east end on league business, Kilmarnock have conceded 13 goals.

It's a ground the Ayrshire side haven't won at since October 2012.

You get the picture. A club - and a manager - with only two wins from their past 11 in all competitions may find it hard to repair fragile confidence in an arena they usually find particularly hostile.

Their season won't be defined by results at Celtic Park, though. It's the games that follow against Aberdeen, St Mirren and Hibs that will determine just how a rocky a road lies ahead, both for Kilmarnock and for McCann.

#826. Kourtney Kardashian's Family Pics Are the Most Interesting to Look At

All the small things are truly what makes Kourtney Kardashian's four-year marriage to Travis Barker the best trip. Want to keep up with the duo and their blended fam? Check out these sweet pics.

Roughly six years ago, Kourtney Kardashian decided to take on a new challenge: Discovering if her longtime friendship with Travis Barker could be a little something more. And, yes, they're doing amazing, sweetie.

Already a mom to Mason Disick, 16, Penelope Disick, 14, and Reign Disick, 11, with ex Scott Disick, welcoming 3-year-old son Rocky Barker with Travis on Nov. 1, 2023, just 18 months after their Italian vows, was "everything I've ever dreamed of," Kourtney shared during a June 2024 episode of The Kardashians. "Everything we've been through to get to this moment, it just feels so surreal."

And with their combined experience, noted the blink-182 drummer—also dad to son Landon Barker, 23, daughter Alabama Barker, 20, and stepdaughter Atiana De La Hoya, 27, with ex-wife Shanna Moakler—life with their youngest has been a joy.

"I loved it when I did it the first time and I love it now," Travis said of parenting in a 2025 chat with Entertainment Tonight. "He’s the coolest little boy. He sleeps all night—10-hour blocks of sleep at night—and he’s up all day playing drums and guitar. I couldn’t be happier."

As for Kourtney, she's very much enjoying the vibe right now.

For the Lemme founder, it's all the big things that makes life with her husband so fantastic. "Grateful, generous, real, raw, dedicated, devoted, family man, talented, survivor, everything… just some of the words used to describe you by those who know you best!" she wrote in a November 2025 Instagram tribute for his 50th birthday. "The leader of our family. My home. You inspire me every single day to be a better person."

And then there's the duet they created together.

"You're such a special soul," Travis wrote on their youngest's second birthday last November, "and you make every day brighter. I love you. No one's cooler. Guitars, drums, pirates, boom boom pow and Angus Young forever."

We, of course, will be keeping up with every last snapshot. ABCDEFG, you have to go check out all the photos the married duo have shared thus far.

#825. Boy hands himself into police after Bradley Lowery taunt in Sunderland match

Coventry fan, 14, had photo of Lowery at Coventry game

Bradley died aged six in 2017 with rare form of cancer

A 14-year-old boy has “handed himself in” to West Midlands police after a video posted on social media appeared to show a Coventry fan taunting Sunderland with a photo of Bradley Lowery during the Premier League match on Saturday.

Sunderland fan Bradley captured the hearts of the football world when he was diagnosed with neuroblastoma, a rare form of childhood cancer. He died aged six in 2017.

Coventry said on Sunday that they were investigating the video footage and Bradley’s mother, Gemma, issued an emotional statement through the Bradley Lowery Foundation, which raises funds and awareness to help and support children.

West Midlands police said: “We are aware of a video circulating on social media showing an incident at Coventry City’s Premier League match with Sunderland [on Saturday] afternoon.

“A thorough investigation has been launched, and a 14-year-old boy has since handed himself in and will be spoken with in due course. We understand the upset and outrage this video has caused in the community and to the victim’s family and our officers are keeping them up to date with the progress of our investigation and working closely alongside both football clubs.”

Coventry said in their earlier statement: “Coventry City FC is aware of footage circulating on social media in connection with an incident during our Premier League fixture against Sunderland. The club does not tolerate offensive behaviour and will liaise with the relevant authorities to determine the appropriate course of action.”

Gemma Lowery said her “beautiful boy deserves to be remembered with love, not hate” in her statement. She posted on Instagram: “Yesterday, a Coventry fan used a photograph of Bradley to taunt Sunderland supporters. As Bradley’s mam, this is heartbreaking, especially as it’s one of my favourite photographs of him. Just look at that smile.

“I remember that day like it was yesterday. He was so happy, having so much fun. Those moments were precious because they were few and far between.

“So much of Bradley’s short life was spent battling cancer and enduring treatments no child should ever face. To see such a beautiful memory used in such a cruel way really does make my heart hurt.

Our picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown in

“We are a football-loving family who follow Sunderland home and away. I’m all for football banter, but surely mocking a child who died from cancer is not banter?”

Lowery added: “I hope the club takes appropriate action and the young lad’s family help him understand how hurtful his actions were. I don’t want hatred directed towards him, so please please don’t, just for him to learn from this.

“Behind that photograph is a little boy who was loved beyond measure and a family who miss him every day. Thank you to everyone who has defended Bradley and shown us so much love. It means more than you know.”

#824. Dylan Efron, Carl Radke & More Celebs to Root for in the NYC Marathon

Feel it comin' in the air. Before the Nov. 1 New York City Marathon brings screams from everywhere, check out which stars—including Dylan Efron, Carl Radke and T.J. Holmes—will hit the ground running.

Count Traitors' Dylan Efron, Summer House's Carl Radke, Dance Moms alum Chloé Lukasiak and actress Jennifer Connelly among those ready to run this town.

As in, lace up their sneaks and sweat their way through all 26.2 miles of the TCS New York City Marathon Nov. 1 in the projected 61-degree temps.

Not that The Challenge star Cory Wharton wasn't already feeling the heat, teaming up with The Children's Heart Foundation for the New York Road Runners race despite having run little more than an hour at a time.

"I'm just happy that I get the chance to run and be a part of this and feel the energy of the crowd," he explained in an exclusive interview with E! News, "and for it to be for a good cause just gives me that much more motivation to get it under five."

And T.J. Lavin will be pleased to know there's no quit in the reality star, inspired to raise funds for those battling heart conditions like his 4-year-old daughter Maya.

"It's just giving me all the motivation that I need," Wharton explained. "I can't wait to FaceTime the girls after finishing and just, 'Look at Daddy's medal.'"

He's not the only celeb with heart, though.

The Bachelorette alum Joe Amabile will be gutting out the run a mere three months after undergoing brain surgery to remove a blueberry-sized lesion.

"I wanted to focus on something positive," he explained to E! News of attempting the journey for a third time. "It helped me so much to put my mindset, not just on focusing on the surgery, because a lot of it was just out of my hands, and the marathon is something that I can control."

Of course, while New York is the concrete jungle where dreams are made of, it's not the only spot where stars can seek that elusive runner's high.

Harry Styles has taken to the streets in his native London, as has Cynthia Erivo. Oprah Winfrey soldiered through Washington, D.C.'s Marine Corps Marathon. And Kevin Hart has covered ground in Chicago while Uzo Aduba and Will Ferrell conquered Boston's Heartbreak Hill.

But come Nov. 1, some 50-plus celebs—including Amabile's fellow Bachelor Nation cohorts Tayshia Adams, Zac Clark, Greg Grippo, Blake Horstmann, Matt James, Hannah Ann Sluss and Andrew Spencer—will slip into an Empire State of mind. As they carb up, check out all of the celebs who have hit the ground running.

The singer was heading in one direction—towards the finish line—at both the 2025 Tokyo Marathon and Berlin Marathon.

"NYC Marathon, round 2!!" the former Bachelorette wrote on Instagram ahead of the 2024 race after having run it three years prior with her former fiancé Zac Clark. "Bib #38793 in hand and ready for the big day! Can’t wait to see you all cheering out there — I’ll need every bit of that energy!"

After finishing the 2024 Chicago Marathon, The Originals star reflected on her journey."I think one of the most important traits in life is humility, but I’m going to let myself feel proud," she wrote on Instagram. "I woke up at 4am all summer to train for this race. It was really f*cking hard and I asked a lot of my family during those 4 months."

"I doubted myself more often than not, and I was sick to my stomach at the thought of letting anyone down," Holt added. "I'm all about breaking mental boundaries," she wrote in a Refinery29 blog post, "and training for a marathon falls right into the Jedi mind-training I need."

Though the Game of Thrones star insisted she didn't care much about her time in the 2016 London Marathon—noting raising upwards of $7,000 for The National Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children's ChildLine service was more important—she admitted to reporters she was "a tiny bit peeved," about her three-hour, 54-minute finish considering it was 24 seconds slower than her 2014 debut.

Running the Boston Marathon in 2015 for the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, the Orange Is the New Black star listened to Sara Bareilles' "Brave" in tribute to a friend she lost to the disease. "That was her motivator getting through every single day of treatment, every single round of chemo, that was what she was listening to constantly," she explained. "And I listen to that when I'm training now, and I can hear her telling me, 'Keep going.'"

Seeing his dad battle Parkinson's disease inspired the Deadpool actor to run the New York City Marathon in 2008. Finishing in three hours, 50 minutes, he also raised money to help fight the disease by teaming up with Michael J. Fox's Team Fox.

After finishing the NYC marathon in 2007, the actress turned up (in heels!) alongside then-husband Tom Cruise for his Lions for Lambs premiere.

"Running a marathon is not a question of whether it will be painful, but when it will be painful," the actor said after finishing his third marathon—Boston's 2003 race—in less than four hours. He later noted to Podium Runner that people "are terribly underwhelmed when they recognize me in a race. There's nothing funny going on. It's just a lot of silence and pain."

After vowing to take on a marathon before she turned 40, the queen of daytime television ran 26.2 miles in Washington, D.C. in 1994. In the pouring rain. As two National Enquirer reporters tagged along tracking her every move. She finished in an impressive four hours, 29 minutes.

Having kept up with the sport long after he ran the Houston course in 1993, Bush accepted few excuses from people who said they simply couldn't squeeze a workout in.

"I believe anyone can make the time [to run]," he told Runner's World during his term. "As a matter of fact, I don't believe it—I know it. If the President of the United States can make the time, anyone can."
